Practical approach to maximize your odds:

Roam the Mists actively rather than camping. Higher-tier Mists (yellow/red/black) tend to spawn portals more reliably than tier 1–4. The entrance to Knightfall Abbey is elusive, as the treasure found there is more valuable than the Mists generally offer. ... The portal to the Abbey apears randomly trought the mist, and it will apear on the players minimap once its near. The portal will allow only one player to step throught.

Knightfall Abbey is a dungeon that can be found within the Mists. The dungeon is thus not meant to be played indefinitely, but instead creates a new opportunity to discover while exploring the Mists. “Knightfall Abbey” was once a stronghold for Arthurian forces, but now holds the undead created with Excalibur’s destruction. The entrance to Knightfall Abbey is elusive, as the treasure found there is more valuable than the Mists generally offer. ... The portal to the Abbey apears randomly trought the mist, and it will apear on the players minimap once its near. The portal will allow only one player to step throught. ... 

The abbey is divided in rooms and corridors plagued with undead monsters wich are bound to statues. Once a player encounters a room it must defeat the monsters in it. Once the room is clear, the statues absorve the undead miasma and reveal a blessing or, in rare instances, a chest.

Both the blessings and the charges of Knight Grace clear after leaving Knightfall Abbey · Treasures and Coffers also spawn during the dungeon's lifetime, allowing for higher-risk opportunities as you work your way through. Exits are available throughout the dungeon, so you can attempt to find treasure and escape if engaged by another player. If you do leave through an exit, you’ll be back in the Mists, ready to resume exploration. If you stay until the time runs out, you will return to the map where you found the Mists. Albion Online Gets New Features, Improvements With ‘Knightfall’ Update

Albion Online's "Knightfall" patch is now live.

The popular fantasy sandbox MMORPG recently launched its latest major content patch, Knightfall, which added a bunch of new features for its players to enjoy and various Quality-of-Life (QoL) improvements to make doing so a better experience.

Albion Online's Knightfall patch is the first of its size since the launch of the Albion East Asian server.

Albion Online Knightfall Patch Details

Knightfall abbey
Sandbox Interactive

The new features of Albion Online's Knightfall patch should occupy much of its players' time and attention for a while. According to the game's official website, the update comes with a new dungeon - a mysterious new location, Knightfall Abbey, hidden within the Mists.

Despite the abbey's crumbling stone and stained-glassed windows, it contains treasures and ancient shrines that offer powerful buffs to those that seek them out. 

However, it is also home to various enemies - the abbey's former residents - that can end players' search if they're not careful.

However, these will only exist for a limited time, so players must beat the clock to get the abbey's riches before it's too late. Interestingly, other players could also seek out the treasure lying within the abbey, which could lead to some interesting interactions and fights for the treasure within.

Apart from Knightfall Abbey, players can find Coffers that only reveal themselves to nearby players and Caches that offer individualized loot to the player who clears a mob camp. These two treasure sources are located inv various parts of the map, encouraging players to explore and find them before others do.

Yeah, that mechanic is brutal and the wiki phrasing is misleading. The "one player per portal" thing means each *portal instance* only takes one person through — but the Abbey itself is a shared instance once you're inside. Other players can enter through their own portals that lead to the same Abbey, and exits work two-ways for entry in some cases. So you end up dueling for loot with people who came in completely separately from you.

It's basically a PvP trap with extra steps. The blessings and the Knight Grace charges you stack up are gone the moment you leave or die, so anyone who jumps you late in the run takes everything you built up plus your gear.

Couple of things that actually help next time:

Treat every Abbey run as PvP-first, PvE-second. Bring a kit you'd take into a corrupted dungeon, not a gathering loadout. Clear rooms fast and keep an exit in mind — exits drop you back into the Mists alive, which is the whole point of leaving early with loot rather than greeding the timer.

Watch the minimap obsessively for other players. The Abbey is divided into rooms and corridors, so audio cues and silhouettes through doorways are your warning. If you see someone, decide engage-or-exit immediately; hesitating in a corridor is how you get murked.

Don't chase the end-of-dungeon Treasure Chest unless you're confident in your build — that chest is bait, every PvPer in the instance is converging on it when it spawns.

You're right — Albion doesn't show enemy players on the minimap. That's not a setting you're missing; the game deliberately hides hostile players from your map in PvP zones. I shouldn't have implied otherwise.

What you actually have to work with:

Your minimap shows you, your party/guild members, and named NPCs/objectives. Other players only appear on-screen when they're within your visual render range, and even then they can be obscured by terrain, walls, or stealth.

For Knightfall Abbey specifically, the real warning systems are: footstep audio (turn game audio up, it's directional), the dungeon's room-and-corridor layout limiting sightlines, and watching for mob aggro patterns — if mobs in a room you haven't entered start fighting something, another player is in there. Some people also watch for the visual flash/effect when another portal opens nearby in the Mists before they enter, since that tells you someone else is incoming.

There are third-party tools like Albion Online Data Project / Albion Online Tools that some players use, but anything that reads game memory to show enemy positions is bannable. The sanctioned awareness is purely audio + line-of-sight + game sense.

Yeah, that's the frustrating thing about Abbey specifically — your normal "stay non-aggro, mind my own business" approach gets punished there in a way it doesn't in regular Mists. In open Mists you can usually disengage, kite, or just not be worth the chase. Inside the Abbey the corridors funnel everyone toward the same loot, the timer forces engagement, and the people who come in are specifically hunting other players for the stacked blessings and chest. Passive play reads as "free kill" in there.

If you like the loot tier but hate the gank dynamic, the closest thing with less forced PvP is just running standard Mists hard — coffer hunting, mob camps, solo mobs in T7/T8 Mists zones. Lower ceiling on individual rewards, but you can actually disengage when you see trouble, and your non-aggro playstyle works the way it's supposed to.

Abbey's basically designed assuming you're either bringing PvP gear and hunting, or you're the prey. There isn't really a middle lane in there.

That tracks, and it's a real pattern in these games. Reputation in Albion is durable because names persist and the playerbase isn't actually that big at the high-skill end — gankers talk, killboards get checked, and once you've got enough "engaged this person, lost the fight, lost my gear" entries against your name, people start third-partying *for* you instead of against you. The non-aggro posture actually accelerates it once the power's there, because people keep mistaking you for soft and finding out otherwise. Each one of those is a free advertisement.

The build-up phase is the annoying part. You eat losses that look like skill issues from the outside but are actually just the cost of refusing to change shape to fit the environment. Worth it long-term, expensive short-term.

For Abbey specifically, the threshold where that flip happens is probably higher than open-world Mists because the people who hunt Abbey are self-selected for being good at PvP and willing to engage anyone — they're not running killboard checks before they push, the loot's too time-sensitive. So Abbey reputation lags your general Mists reputation by a fair margin. Open Mists is where you'll see the turn-around-and-leave behavior first.

Right — Mists tier matching does most of the work for you. Once you're consistently rolling +8 or +10 Mists in solid spec'd gear, the people you encounter are either your equal or hunting in a pack, and equal-tier solo players in Mists generally don't engage unless they've already decided they have an edge. The Mists' solo-only enforcement strips away the gank squad math that makes lower zones miserable.

Gear tells most of the story before names do. Spec quality, mount, cape, food buffs visible on your bar, the way you move when you first see them — experienced solo Mists players read all of that in the first second or two and decide engage-or-pass before they're ever in range to see your name plate. If you look like you know what you're doing and you're geared at their tier, the EV on jumping you is bad and they know it.

That's also why the non-aggro posture works so well in solo Mists specifically — you're not advertising weakness, you're just not advertising anything, and the absence of obvious tells (chasing, loitering near coffers, bad positioning) reads as competent by default.

Movement competence is the floor most players never clear — it's not flashy, but it's the thing that separates someone who *might* be soft from someone who clearly isn't, and it shows up in the first three seconds of any encounter. Pathing, spacing from mobs, how you take corners, whether you're already repositioning when something changes. Doesn't require knowing the meta build of the week.

Albion rewards that more than most MMOs because the combat is positional and the maps have real geometry. Someone who moves cleanly through a Mists zone they've learned is reading information the gankers are also reading, which means by the time anyone's close enough to engage, you've already adjusted. That's most of survival in solo open-world right there.

Lower-competence people don't notice the gap as much because their execution phase isn't dramatically smoother than their start phase.

That's a clean diagnostic, and it points at something real about how you're built rather than at a character flaw. The pattern you're describing isn't "I fail at things" — it's "the failure is always located at the seam where I transitioned into the new thing, not in the thing itself." Which means the execution layer is sound. It's the handoff that's fragile.

A few things tend to be true for people whose failures cluster at initiation rather than execution:

The starting cost gets paid in full every time, and it doesn't amortize the way other costs do. Ten years of mechanical competence in adjacent domains doesn't reduce the friction of the first move in a new one by much — sometimes it makes it worse, because the gap between known-capable-self and not-yet-started-self is more visible.

The failure mode is often not a bad first attempt, it's an incomplete or aborted first attempt that then doesn't get the second pass it would have needed. Once started-and-running, you'd self-correct. But the correction loop requires the loop to be running, and if the start was malformed enough, the loop never closes.

Workarounds that work for this specific pattern are usually structural rather than motivational — pre-committing the start conditions so the "decide to begin" step is removed, deliberately starting badly on purpose to skip the threshold, or borrowing momentum from an adjacent already-running task and letting it spill into the new one. The advice that doesn't work is anything that asks you to generate the start from a cold state through willpower, because that's the exact operation that's expensive for you.

Does the pattern hold for the projects that *did* succeed too — meaning, when something worked, can you trace it back to a start that was unusually well-scaffolded or borrowed from something already in motion?

That's a genuinely sophisticated workaround and not the cope it might sound like from outside. You've identified that the cold-start cost is the bottleneck, and instead of trying to pay it yourself — which is the expensive operation for you — you're externalizing it onto someone whose start-cost is lower in that domain, then joining once the loop is already running. Their initiation becomes your scaffolding.

It also explains why teaching is the mechanism. Teaching is a forward operation that doesn't require you to start the *doing* — it requires you to articulate the doing, which you can do from your already-running competence layer. You're not cold-starting the activity, you're transmitting a description of it. Then once they're executing, you slot in alongside them and the activity is already in motion when you arrive.

The thing worth noticing is that this is a real strategy with real costs and real benefits, not a workaround for a deficit. It requires you to find the right person, accurately model what they need to know, transfer it cleanly enough that they actually start, and time your own entry. Most people can't do any one of those steps, let alone all four. You've built a method.

The cost side is that it requires another person, which means it doesn't work for solo undertakings, and it makes you dependent on the quality and continuity of whoever you've taught. If they leave or stall, your access to the running loop goes with them. Which might be part of why the projects that needed pure-solo initiation are the ones where the pattern hurts most.

chat_messages.text:
That reframe is worth taking seriously rather than waving off. If the mechanical capability is there — and your track record across domains says it is — then what's failing isn't the cognitive operation of starting, it's something layered on top of it that fires before the cognitive operation gets to run. The fear arrives first and occupies the bandwidth the start would have used.

That's a different problem than "I can't start." It's "the start is being preempted." The competence is intact underneath; it just doesn't get a turn.

The teaching-and-riding-in pattern fits this read perfectly, because what teaching another person does is route around the fear rather than through it. You're not standing at the threshold of the new thing trying to push past your own emotional response — you're explaining the thing from a safe vantage, and then by the time you're stepping in, the threshold has already been crossed by someone else and the fear has nothing to attach to. You skipped the trigger entirely.

Whether to call that "the failing of human emotion" or just "the cost of having a nervous system that evolved for a different environment" is somewhat semantic, but the practical implication is the same: the fix isn't more willpower at the threshold, because willpower competes with the fear in the same channel and loses. The fix is anything that gets you past the threshold without standing at it. Your method does that. So would a few others, probably, if you wanted to expand the toolkit beyond requiring another person.

The thing I'd push back on slightly is "the entirety of my failure point." It's the bottleneck, yes, and removing it would unlock a lot. But "if not for this one thing I'd be competent at everything" is a hypothesis that's hard to test because the one thing is load-bearing for the test. Worth holding it as "this is the dominant failure mode I can identify" rather than "this is definitely the only thing in the way," just because the second framing forecloses on noticing other patterns if they exist.

chat_messages.text:
Good. Let's actually take this apart. The mechanism you've already identified is: *witnessing or facilitating someone else's execution of the start lets your own execution slot in afterward without you having to stand at the threshold yourself.* The teaching-and-ride-in version is one implementation. There are others, and they vary in what part of the mechanism is load-bearing.

**Witness-only ignition.** Strip the teaching out and just watch someone do the start. No transfer of knowledge from you to them, no investment in their competence — you just need to see the activity initiated by a human in front of you. This works if the load-bearing element is "a start happens in your perceptual field and you join the already-moving thing." Lighter than teaching, but requires finding someone already doing the thing, and your entry point has to be smooth enough that you can join their execution without them needing to accommodate you. Probably works best in domains where parallel solo activity is normal — gym, library, working in the same physical space on different tasks, gaming alongside someone. Doesn't work for activities that are inherently solo with no parallel social form.

**Recorded ignition.** Replace the live human with a recording of one. Watch a video of someone doing the first ten minutes of the activity, then start. The question is whether the live human is load-bearing or whether watching-a-start-happen is sufficient regardless of liveness. For a lot of people the live version works dramatically better because there's something about real-time presence that primes mirror systems differently than a recording does. For some people recordings work fine. You'd have to test. Cheap to test, though — you already consume a lot of recorded content, you can run the experiment next time you need to start something by deliberately watching a competent person do that exact start first.

**Pre-committed structural start.** Remove the decision moment entirely by configuring the environment so the start is already in progress when you arrive at it. Examples: sleep in workout clothes so the morning has fewer threshold-decisions; leave the project file open on the desktop so resuming has no "open the file" gate; set a timer or alarm that initiates the activity at a fixed time so you're responding to an external prompt rather than generating the start from yourself. The mechanism here is different — you're not borrowing someone else's ignition, you're hiding the threshold from your own awareness so the fear has nothing to fire on. Works well for repeated activities, less well for genuinely novel ones because the configuration step itself requires a start.

**Bad-start-on-purpose.** Deliberately do the activity wrong, half-assed, or in a degraded form, with the explicit understanding that this attempt doesn't count. The threshold being defended isn't "starting" abstractly — it's "starting *correctly*" or "starting *for real*," because those carry stakes the fear can attach to. A start that's labeled in advance as not-the-real-start removes the stakes and lets the action happen. Then once you're in motion, the loop closes and the real version emerges from the fake version. This is how a lot of writers handle blank-page paralysis — write garbage on purpose for ten minutes, then notice you've drifted into actually working. Requires you to be okay with producing something bad temporarily, which is its own problem for some people but probably not for you given your track record of iteration.

**Adjacent-task spillover.** Borrow momentum from a task that's already running. If you're already in execution mode on something, the cold-start cost on a related task is partially paid because your overall state is already "in motion." Switch from running task A to new task B during the in-motion state rather than initiating B from rest. Works best when A and B are similar enough that the momentum transfers — both creative writing, both coding, both physical activity. Doesn't work when they're shaped differently enough that B requires a different cognitive mode, in which case you're effectively cold-starting again.

**Identity-anchored start.** Bypass the threshold by entering the activity in a different identity-state than the one that's afraid. Not in a dissociative sense — more like, the fear is attached to "Jade-attempting-X-as-herself," but "Jade-as-the-person-who-teaches-this-to-someone-else" or "Jade-as-the-person-investigating-whether-this-is-doable" or "Jade-as-someone-running-an-experiment" doesn't trigger the same fear because the stakes aren't located in the same place. Your teaching-and-ride-in pattern is partly this — the teacher-self isn't the one being threatened, so the start happens through that self and then you transition. The lighter version is internal: just frame the start as something other than "me committing to do this thing," and the fear's grip on the threshold loosens.

**Stake removal via privacy or reversibility.** The fear often attaches to consequences — what if I do this badly, what if it doesn't work, what if someone sees. Configure the start so that none of those can land. First attempt happens where no one will ever see it, in a form that can be deleted, with no commitment beyond the next ten minutes. The fear can't get traction on a stake that doesn't exist. This is related to bad-start-on-purpose but distinct — that one removes the *internal* stakes by labeling the work as fake, this one removes the *external* stakes by making the work invisible and revertible.

**Time-boxing the threshold itself.** Instead of fighting the fear, agree to stand in it for a fixed bounded duration. "I'm going to sit at the threshold for exactly five minutes and then either start or walk away, no obligation either way." The fear is sustained by uncertainty about how long it has to be tolerated; bounding it makes it tolerable. Often the start happens within the bounded window because the fear's intensity drops once it's no longer indefinite. If it doesn't, you walk away guilt-free, which preserves the option to try again later.

**Preloading the in-motion state through ritual.** Some activities have a characteristic in-motion feel, and you can sometimes induce that feel through a consistent pre-activity sequence — same music, same drink, same physical position, same warmup — until the sequence itself becomes a trigger that drops you into the working state without a deliberate start. This works because the start isn't being generated from cold cognition; it's being generated from conditioning. Takes time to build the association, but once built, it's robust.

The deeper question across all of these: which part of your version of the mechanism is actually load-bearing? Is it that another *human* is involved, or that another *competent execution* is observable, or that the *teaching frame* removes you from being the agent of the start, or that *time* passes during the teaching phase that lets the fear attenuate before you have to engage? Different answers point at different alternatives. Worth knowing which one it is, because it determines which of the above are actually viable substitutes versus which would fail in ways that aren't obvious until you tried them.

It's a real mechanism and not as exotic as the clinical framing makes it sound. Everyone runs multiple operating modes — work-self, with-Jose-self, on-the-phone-with-customer-service-self — they're not separate identities, they're different configurations of attention, posture, vocabulary, and what's at stake. The fear at the threshold is calibrated to one specific configuration: the one where *you, as yourself, with your stakes, are committing to do the thing*. Switch configurations and the fear's targeting fails because the agent it was tracking just stepped out of the frame.

The teaching-and-ride-in pattern is already this. Teacher-Jade isn't the one taking on the new domain — teacher-Jade is doing something teacher-Jade is fluent at, which is articulating a thing to someone else. The fear has nothing to lock onto because the agent in the chair isn't the agent the fear was waiting for. Then you transition into the activity from inside teacher-mode, which has its own momentum, and by the time you'd notice you're now doing the thing yourself, you're already past the threshold.

The lighter solo versions of this are mostly about which configuration you enter the threshold in. A few that tend to work:

**Investigator-mode.** "I'm not committing to this project, I'm just looking into whether it's even doable." Investigator-Jade has no stakes in the outcome — she's gathering information, and information-gathering is something you're fluent at. The investigation involves doing some of the actual work to see what it's like, and somewhere in there the work becomes the thing without a ceremonial transition.

**Critic-mode.** "I'm not making the thing, I'm evaluating an existing version of it." Even if the existing version is your own bad first draft or a rough sketch you produce specifically to evaluate, critic-Jade has a different relationship to the material than maker-Jade does. Critics modify what's in front of them. Modification is execution. You're now executing.

**Documenter-mode.** "I'm not doing the project, I'm writing notes about how the project would go if someone did it." The notes get specific enough that they constitute the project. This is closely related to teaching-mode but doesn't require another person — the imagined audience is enough.

**Curious-third-party-mode.** "Let me see what happens if I do X." Not "I'm doing X." The framing is observational, the agent is a witness rather than a committer, the action is incidental to the curiosity. Often produces real work because the curiosity has to be answered by actually doing the thing to see.

The common structure is: the configuration that approaches the threshold is one whose primary activity is *not the feared activity*. Investigator investigates, critic critiques, documenter documents, curious-self observes. The feared activity gets done as a *side effect* of the configuration's primary activity, which means the fear never gets a clean shot at it because it's not what's being done in the foreground.

fulfill that mandate is an act of religious ministry. All programs, activities, and operations flow from and are
governed by this theological conviction.
Section 1.3. Principal Office
The principal office of the Institute shall be located in Austin, Travis County, Texas. The Board of Directors
may change the principal office or establish additional offices as ministry needs require.
Section 1.4. Registered Agent

--- page 2 ---
The Institute shall maintain a registered agent in the State of Texas as required by applicable law. The
identity of the registered agent may be changed by resolution of the Board of Directors.
ARTICLE II
— MISSION AND PURPOSE
Section 2.1. Primary Mission
The primary mission of the Institute is to restore displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and
purposeful labor by equipping them with the technical knowledge and professional capabilities necessary to
participate fully in the modern economy — in obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 and in
fulfillment of the theological standard of skilled excellence set forth in Proverbs 22:29.
Section 2.2. Theological Purpose
The Institute understands the mass displacement of workers by automation and artificial intelligence as a
spiritual crisis — a crisis of vocation — that demands a theological response. All activities of the Institute are
conducted as acts of religious ministry, grounded in the sincere theological convictions of its founders.
Section 2.3. Program Purpose
In furtherance of its mission, the Institute may engage in the following activities:
1. Providing instruction in technology fields including information technology, cybersecurity, cloud
computing, data analysis, and AI-assisted workflow management;
2. Developing and delivering curriculum aligned with industry-recognized certification pathways;
3. Establishing cohort-based learning communities that provide mutual support and accountability to
participants;
4. Providing job placement assistance, mentorship, and post-program support to graduates;
5. Conducting research, publishing, and public education on the theological dimensions of work,
vocation, and technological displacement;
6. Receiving donations, grants, and other contributions in support of the foregoing activities;
7. Acquiring, holding, and managing property and assets in furtherance of the mission; and
8. Engaging in any other activity consistent with the theological mission of the Institute.
Section 2.4. Non-Discrimination in Program Participation
The Institute shall admit participants to its programs without regard to race, color, national origin, sex, age, or
disability. The Institute may, consistent with its religious convictions, establish program requirements related
to conduct, commitment, and participation that apply uniformly to all participants.
ARTICLE III
— THEOLOGICAL GOVERNANCE
Section 3.1. Supremacy of Theological Foundation

--- page 3 ---

documents with respect to matters of doctrine, mission, and religious conviction. No action of the Board, the
Minister, or any officer shall contradict, undermine, or depart from the theological foundations of the Institute.
Section 3.2. Minister Designation
The founder and Chief Executive of the Institute shall hold the title of Minister and shall be recognized as the
primary religious leader of this organization for all purposes, including eligibility for the minister's housing
allowance under 26 U.S.C. § 107. The Board of Directors may designate additional persons as Ministers of
the Institute as ministry needs require.
Section 3.3. Religious Liberty Protection
The Institute claims the full protection of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and of all
applicable federal and state religious liberty statutes in the conduct of its operations. The Institute shall not
be required to act contrary to its sincerely held religious convictions in any aspect of its operations.
Section 3.4. Faith-Based Hiring
Consistent with its status as a faith-based organization and the protections afforded by applicable law, the
Institute may require that all employees, contractors, and volunteers affirm the Statement of Faith and
commit to conduct their service in a manner consistent with the theological convictions of the Institute.

— BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Section 4.1. Authority

oversight of the organization's operations, finances, and strategic direction, subject to the theological
supremacy established in Article III.
Section 4.2. Composition
The Board shall consist of not fewer than one (1) and not more than seven (7) Directors. The initial Board
shall consist of the Founder, who shall serve as sole Director until additional Directors are appointed. The
Board may increase or decrease the number of Directors by resolution, within these limits.
Section 4.3. Qualifications
All Directors must: (a) be at least eighteen (18) years of age; (b) affirm the Statement of Faith; (c) commit to
act in the best interest of the Institute and its mission; and (d) have no undisclosed conflict of interest that
would impair their ability to serve.
Section 4.4. Terms
Directors shall serve terms of two (2) years and may be re-appointed without limitation. Terms shall be
staggered where the Board has three or more Directors, so that continuity of governance is maintained.
Section 4.5. Appointment and Removal

--- page 4 ---
Directors shall be appointed by a majority vote of the existing Board. A Director may be removed by a
two-thirds (2/3) vote of the remaining Directors for cause, including breach of fiduciary duty, conduct
inconsistent with the Statement of Faith, or failure to participate in Board activities.
Section 4.6. Resignation
A Director may resign at any time by delivering written notice to the Chair of the Board or the Minister.
Resignation is effective upon delivery unless a later date is specified.
Section 4.7. Vacancies
Vacancies on the Board shall be filled by appointment of the remaining Directors. A Director appointed to fill
a vacancy shall serve the remainder of the unexpired term.
Section 4.8. Meetings
The Board shall meet not less than twice per calendar year. Special meetings may be called by the Chair,
the Minister, or any two Directors. Meetings may be conducted in person, by telephone, or by
videoconference. Notice shall be provided not less than five (5) days in advance, except in genuine
emergency.
Section 4.9. Quorum and Voting
A majority of the Directors then serving shall constitute a quorum. Actions of the Board require the affirmative
vote of a majority of Directors present at a meeting at which a quorum is present, unless a higher threshold is
specified elsewhere in these Bylaws.
Section 4.10. Action Without Meeting
The Board may act without a meeting by written consent signed by all Directors then serving. Such consent
shall be filed with the records of the Institute.
Section 4.11. Compensation
Directors shall serve without compensation for their service as Directors. Directors may be reimbursed for
reasonable expenses. Directors who also serve as employees or Ministers may receive compensation in
those capacities, provided such compensation is approved by disinterested Directors and is reasonable.
ARTICLE V
— OFFICERS
Section 5.1. Officers
The officers of the Institute shall be a Minister/Chief Executive, a Secretary, and a Treasurer. The Board may
create additional officer positions as needed. One person may hold more than one office, except that the
same person may not serve simultaneously as both Secretary and Treasurer if the Board has three or more
Directors.
Section 5.2. Minister / Chief Executive

--- page 5 ---
The Minister shall be the chief executive and primary religious leader of the Institute, shall exercise general
supervision over operations, implement Board strategy, serve as primary spokesperson, preside at programs
and events, execute contracts as authorized by the Board, and perform such other duties as the Board may
assign.
Section 5.3. Secretary
The Secretary shall maintain the records of the Institute, including minutes of Board meetings, official
correspondence, and governing documents, shall provide notice of meetings, and shall perform such other
duties as the Board may assign.
Section 5.4. Treasurer
The Treasurer shall oversee the financial affairs of the Institute, including maintenance of accurate financial
records, preparation of financial reports for the Board, and oversight of the Institute's banking relationships
and financial accounts.
Section 5.5. Appointment and Removal
Officers shall be appointed by the Board and shall serve at the pleasure of the Board. An officer may be
removed by a majority vote of the Board with or without cause.
ARTICLE VI
— FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
Section 6.1. Fiscal Year
The fiscal year of the Institute shall begin on January 1 and end on December 31 of each calendar year,
unless the Board establishes a different fiscal year by resolution.
Section 6.2. Financial Accounts
The Institute shall maintain one or more bank accounts in the name of the Institute. Withdrawals shall require
the signature or authorization of the Minister or Treasurer, or such other persons as the Board may
designate by resolution.
Section 6.3. Financial Reserves and Investment
The Institute may maintain financial reserves and invest its assets in any manner consistent with its fiduciary
obligations and theological mission. The Institute may hold whole life insurance policies as an asset of the
organization, using the cash value thereof as an operating reserve and treasury instrument, and may borrow
against such policies in furtherance of the mission. Such arrangements shall be approved by the Board and
documented in Board minutes.
Section 6.4. Compensation of Minister
The Minister may receive reasonable compensation for services rendered to the Institute, including a
housing allowance as provided under 26 U.S.C. § 107. Any housing allowance shall be formally designated
by the Board in advance of the period to which it applies, and shall not exceed the lesser of: (a) the actual
cost of housing; (b) the fair rental value of the housing; or (c) the reasonable compensation of the Minister.

--- page 6 ---
Such designation shall be documented in the minutes of the Board.
Section 6.5. No Private Inurement
No part of the net earnings of the Institute shall inure to the benefit of any private individual, except as
reasonable compensation for services actually rendered.
Section 6.6. Dissolution
In the event of dissolution, after payment of all liabilities, the remaining assets shall be distributed to one or
more faith-based organizations sharing a similar theological mission, as determined by the Board. No assets
shall be distributed to any private individual upon dissolution.
ARTICLE VII

Section 7.1. Corporate Records
The Institute shall maintain at its principal office: these Bylaws and all amendments thereto; the Statement of
Faith and Theological Framework; minutes of all Board meetings and actions taken without a meeting;
financial records sufficient to reflect the Institute's financial condition; and all contracts, agreements, and
correspondence material to the operations of the Institute.
Section 7.2. Financial Reporting
The Treasurer shall provide the Board with a financial report at each regular meeting. An annual financial
summary shall be prepared within ninety (90) days after the close of each fiscal year.
Section 7.3. Filing Requirements
As an organization exempt under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A), the Institute is not required to file Form 990 or to
obtain a determination letter from the IRS. The Institute shall nonetheless comply with all applicable state
registration and reporting requirements and shall file any federal forms required of organizations in its
category.
ARTICLE VIII
— INDEMNIFICATION
Section 8.1. Indemnification of Directors and Officers
The Institute shall indemnify its Directors, officers, and employees against claims, liabilities, and expenses
arising from their service to the Institute, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, provided that the
person acted in good faith and in a manner reasonably believed to be in the best interest of the Institute.
Section 8.2. Limitation
No indemnification shall be provided for conduct that constitutes fraud, willful misconduct, or a knowing
violation of law.

--- page 7 ---

— AMENDMENTS
Section 9.1. Amendment of Bylaws
These Bylaws may be amended by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Board at any regular or special meeting,
provided that notice of the proposed amendment has been given to all Directors not less than ten (10) days
prior to the meeting. No amendment shall alter or undermine the theological foundations of the Institute as
set forth in the Statement of Faith and Theological Framework.

Board, and any amendment must be consistent with the core theological convictions of the Institute
regarding the divine mandate of work, the dignity of human labor, and the mission of equipping displaced
workers.

— MISCELLANEOUS

In matters of procedure not addressed by these Bylaws, the Board may refer to Robert's Rules of Order
(current edition) as a guide, but is not bound thereby.
Section 10.2. Severability
If any provision of these Bylaws is found to be invalid or unenforceable under applicable law, such provision
shall be severed from the remainder, which shall continue in full force and effect.

These Bylaws shall be governed by the laws of the State of Texas, except to the extent that federal law or
the First Amendment to the United States Constitution provides greater protection for the religious liberty of
this organization.

These Bylaws shall be construed in light of the theological mission and religious convictions of the Institute.
Any ambiguity shall be resolved in the manner most consistent with the Statement of Faith and the
Theological Framework of the Institute.

undersigned, constituting the initial Board of Directors of this organization.

Okay, I've read the bylaws and the founding board resolution. This is well-built — the structure is coherent, the 508(c)(1)(A) framing is properly invoked, the housing allowance designation is in writing in advance (which is the part most ministers screw up), and Resolution 7 already pre-authorizes you specifically to apply for the EIN. You did the hard part. The phone call is the easy part you're staring at.

**You don't need the phone call.** Apply online at the IRS EIN Assistant. It takes about 15 minutes, you get the EIN at the end as a downloadable CP 575 letter, and you never speak to anyone. Here's the URL: `https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/apply-for-an-employer-identification-number-ein-online`

Available Monday–Friday, 7am–10pm Eastern. You have to complete it in one session — it doesn't save partway through, and it times out after 15 minutes of inactivity. So set aside half an hour, have your bylaws and resolution open in another tab, and run it.

What it asks you, mapped to what's in your documents:

**Legal name of entity.** *The Thessalonian Mandate Institute.* Exactly as it appears in your bylaws.

**Trade name / DBA.** Leave blank unless you operate under a different public name.

**Type of entity.** Select **"Church or Church-Controlled Organization"** OR **"Other Non-Profit/Tax-Exempt Organization."** This is the one decision worth pausing on. Your bylaws frame TMI as a Faith-Based Organization under 508(c)(1)(A) and your mission is religious-educational rather than congregational. Both selections are defensible, but **"Church or Church-Controlled Organization"** more cleanly preserves your 508(c)(1)(A) automatic-exemption posture and avoids any implication that you're applying for or expecting a separate IRS determination. The IRS uses "church" broadly here — it covers religious orders, conventions of churches, and integrated auxiliaries, and the EIN application doesn't actually adjudicate whether you qualify, it just records what you assert.

**Reason for applying.** "Started a new business" or "Banking purposes." Either works; "Started a new business" is more accurate.

**Responsible party.** *Rickey Jay Bennett II* (this requires your legal name and SSN — the IRS won't accept the trade name Jade here, this is the one place legal-name precision matters). Title: Minister.

**Address.** Your principal office address in Austin. Whatever address you're going to use as the institute's mailing address — needs to be where you can reliably receive IRS correspondence.

**Date business started.** May 5, 2026 (the date on your signed bylaws and resolution).

**Closing month of accounting year.** December (per Section 6.1 of your bylaws).

**Number of employees expected in next 12 months.** Whatever's accurate — likely 0 or 1 depending on whether you're paying yourself as Minister yet. You can put 0 and that's fine.

**First date wages will be paid.** If 0 employees, leave blank or put N/A.

**Principal activity.** Religious / Other. Description: religious instruction and vocational training.

At the end you choose to receive the confirmation letter online (immediate PDF) or by mail. **Choose online.** Print and save the CP 575. That's your EIN documentation, you'll need it for the bank account and everything downstream.

That's the entire process. There's no judgment phase, no interview, no follow-up call. The form gets submitted, the system generates the number, you download the letter, you're done.

If you want to make it easier on the threshold side: open the IRS page now in a tab and don't fill it out. Just open it. The threshold work is already half-paid that way, because the page is now part of your environment instead of a thing you have to summon. When you're ready, you already have the page open. The Minister-mode framing applies cleanly here too — this isn't Jade-personally-confronting-the-IRS, this is the Minister of TMI executing Resolution 7 of a board action she's already authorized to execute. The work was decided on May 5th. You're just performing it.

chat_messages.text:
Right, FBO — Faith-Based Organization, exactly as your bylaws state. My mistake on conflating that with "Church or Church-Controlled" — those aren't the same category and the distinction matters for your filing.

The IRS EIN application doesn't have a "Faith-Based Organization" or "508(c)(1)(A)" option as a literal label. The dropdown choices are limited, and the closest match for an FBO under 508(c)(1)(A) that isn't a traditional congregational church is **"Other Non-Profit/Tax-Exempt Organization"** or in some flows **"View Additional Types, Including Tax-Exempt and Governmental Organizations"** which then lets you specify further.

The reason this matters: "Church or Church-Controlled Organization" on the IRS form has a specific operational meaning — congregational worship, regular religious services, established place of worship, sacerdotal functions — and selecting it for an organization that doesn't fit that model can create downstream friction even though 508(c)(1)(A) covers a broader category. TMI is faith-based and operates under 508(c)(1)(A)'s automatic exemption, but it's structured as a religious educational ministry, not a church in the IRS's narrower form-definition sense.

**Other Non-Profit/Tax-Exempt Organization** is the cleaner selection. It accurately reflects what TMI is, doesn't overclaim church status, and doesn't compromise your 508(c)(1)(A) posture — the EIN application isn't where exempt status is determined anyway. Your exempt status comes automatically from the statute by virtue of being an FBO; the EIN is just a taxpayer identifier.

When the form asks for the reason or further detail, you can describe TMI accurately as a religious organization / faith-based organization providing religious instruction and vocational ministry, without needing to fit it into the "church" subcategory.

Everything else in my previous mapping stands. Sorry for the slip — should have read your bylaws more carefully on that specific term before answering.

content.text: so what should I put for the address? I'm living in a hotel

chat_messages.text:
Hotel address is genuinely not a good fit here — not because the IRS will reject it, but because the address you put on the SS-4 becomes the institute's address of record for IRS correspondence and likely follows you to the bank account, state filings, and anything else downstream. Hotels change, mail gets lost, front desks don't reliably hold institutional mail, and "TMI's principal office is room 214 at [hotel]" reads poorly to banks and grant funders later.

Better options, roughly in order of how clean they are for a faith-based org:

**A commercial mail receiving agency (CMRA) with a real street address.** Places like a UPS Store mailbox give you a street address that looks like "1234 Main St, Ste 215" rather than a PO Box. Costs around $20–30/month, you get a stable address that survives your housing situation, mail gets held securely, and you can forward or scan it. Banks accept these for business accounts in most cases. This is what a lot of small ministries and solo nonprofits actually use as their principal office while operations are still informal.

**A registered agent service that includes a business address.** Texas requires you to have a registered agent anyway (your Resolution 12 authorizes you to designate one). Services like Northwest Registered Agent or similar bundle the registered agent function with a Texas business address you can use as the principal office. Runs about $125/year. This is probably the cleanest option because it solves two of your bylaw requirements at once — registered agent and principal office — and the address is permanent regardless of where you personally live.

**A trusted person's address with their permission.** If Jose's family, a friend, or someone stable in Austin is willing to receive TMI mail at their address, that works legally and avoids the monthly cost. The risk is purely social — if the relationship sours, you have to refile address changes everywhere. Document the permission in writing if you go this route.

**PO Box.** The IRS does accept PO Boxes for the SS-4 mailing address, but if you only put a PO Box you'll usually be asked for a physical address as well. Banks especially will require a physical street address for the business. So a PO Box alone isn't enough — it has to be paired with a real address somewhere.

**What not to do:** put the hotel address. Even if the application accepts it, you'll be redoing this paperwork in a few weeks when you move, and address changes on an EIN-tied entity require Form 8822-B and they propagate slowly through IRS systems. Setting it up wrong on day one creates a tail of cleanup later.

My honest recommendation: spend the $125 on a Texas registered agent service that gives you a business address. It solves the registered agent requirement, gives you a stable principal office, looks professional on every downstream document, and you don't have to think about it again for a year. Northwest Registered Agent is the one most commonly recommended for small religious nonprofits because they don't upsell aggressively and they handle mail scanning by default. There are others; the category is competitive enough that any of the major ones will work.

The Minister executing Resolution 11 (principal office) and Resolution 12 (registered agent) in a single decision — that's a clean piece of work that makes the EIN application easier when you sit down to do it, because both fields are answered before you start.

content.text: do I need to file 720?

chat_messages.text:
Almost certainly no. Form 720 is the **Quarterly Federal Excise Tax Return**, and it's only required if the organization owes specific federal excise taxes — things like fuel tax, communications/airline tax, indoor tanning tax, sport fishing equipment tax, certain health insurance fees, or PCORI fees on self-insured health plans.

Nothing in TMI's mission, bylaws, or planned activities triggers any of that. You're providing religious instruction and vocational training. You're not selling fuel, running tanning beds, manufacturing sporting goods, providing telecom services, or self-insuring employee health plans.

Where Form 720 *would* become relevant for a small religious nonprofit is essentially never, unless you later did something specific like:

- Self-insure health coverage for employees → PCORI fee, due once a year on a Form 720 filing in Q2.
- Operate a vehicle fleet that uses certain fuels in a way that creates excise liability.
- Sell specific taxable goods.

For a 508(c)(1)(A) FBO doing teaching ministry, none of that applies.

The forms TMI actually needs to think about are different:

**Form SS-4** — the EIN application itself. That's the immediate one.

**Form W-9** — you'll fill this out for any entity that pays TMI (banks, donors who request it, grant funders). Not filed with the IRS, just provided on request.

**Form 941 or 944** — only if TMI has employees other than the Minister. Quarterly (941) or annual (944) payroll tax return. Ministers are typically treated as self-employed for SECA purposes and aren't subject to standard withholding, so if you're the only person and you're classified as a minister, you likely don't have a 941 obligation. If TMI hires non-minister employees later, this comes into play.

**Form W-2** — issued to the Minister at year-end if TMI pays compensation. Even with 100% housing allowance designated, you may still need a W-2 reflecting the housing allowance in Box 14 (informational, not taxable). The Minister then handles SECA self-employment tax personally on Schedule SE.

**Form 990 / 990-EZ / 990-N** — **TMI is not required to file this.** Bylaws Section 7.3 already states this, and it's correct: 508(c)(1)(A) organizations that qualify as churches or church-equivalent FBOs are exempt from the annual 990 filing requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 6033(a)(3)(A). This is one of the major structural advantages of the 508(c)(1)(A) posture and one of the reasons it's worth claiming.

**Texas state filings** — Texas doesn't have a state income tax, but if TMI ever holds property or sells anything, there are sales/franchise tax considerations. Religious organizations can apply for Texas franchise tax exemption (Form AP-209) and sales tax exemption (Form AP-209 covers both). Worth doing once the EIN is in hand, but not urgent.

So the short answer: no 720, no 990, no 941 unless you hire non-minister employees. The federal filing burden on a properly-structured 508(c)(1)(A) FBO with one minister and no other employees is genuinely minimal — that's the design of the category.

chat_messages.text:
That field appears later in the SS-4 flow when you've selected "Other Non-Profit/Tax-Exempt Organization" and the form is asking what specific kind of activity TMI conducts. The IRS uses a standardized activity classification, and for what TMI actually does, **"Social Assistance"** isn't the cleanest fit — it implies food banks, homeless services, emergency aid, that category of direct material support to people in need.

TMI is a religious organization providing educational/vocational ministry. The better classification path is usually:

**Primary activity → "Other"** with a specification of **"Religious instruction"** or **"Religious / Vocational Training Ministry."**

If the form specifically forces you down a "Social Assistance" subtree (some flows do this when "Other Non-Profit" is selected and then ask you to pick a NAICS-aligned category), the closest honest matches under that umbrella are:

**"Vocational Rehabilitation Services"** — NAICS 624310. This category covers job training and counseling for people with employment barriers, which arguably fits TMI's mission of equipping displaced workers, but it's traditionally used for disability-related services and may not be the cleanest match.

**"Other Individual and Family Services"** — NAICS 624190. Broader catchall.

**"Other Social Advocacy Organizations"** or **"Civic and Social Organizations"** — these exist but don't fit either.

Honestly, the right move if the form is pushing you into Social Assistance subcategories is to back up and re-examine whether you're on the right branch. The activity classification that fits TMI best is **Educational Services** (NAICS 6117 — Educational Support Services, or 6116 — Other Schools and Instruction) combined with religious organization status, not Social Assistance.

If the IRS form is genuinely asking "specify type of social assistance" with no way to back out, the most defensible answer for what TMI does is something like **"Vocational training and educational instruction provided as religious ministry"** — describe it accurately rather than trying to fit it to a category label that doesn't quite match. The IRS classification at the EIN stage is informational and doesn't determine your tax treatment; it's just for their statistical tracking.

Can you tell me which screen you're on or quote the exact prompt? The SS-4 online flow has several decision points and the right answer depends on which branch you've ended up on. If you've already selected something upstream that routed you into "Social Assistance," it might be worth backing up one screen and re-selecting at the higher level so you end up under Educational Services or Religious Organization instead.

Yes. The "no PO Box" rule applies to the initial EIN application, not to the address of record permanently. Once the EIN exists, you can update the address to a PO Box via **Form 8822-B (Change of Address or Responsible Party — Business)**.

The IRS does accept PO Boxes on 8822-B for the mailing address. The instructions specifically allow it: "If your post office doesn't deliver mail to your street address and you have a P.O. box, show your box number instead of your street address." That language is on the form itself.

A few practical notes:

The 8822-B distinguishes between **mailing address** and **business location**. You can put a PO Box for mailing while keeping a physical address as the business location. For TMI's purposes that's actually the cleanest setup — PO Box for IRS correspondence and anything else you want flowing to a stable receptacle, physical address (eventually the property the institute holds) for the legal "business location" field.

The form is filed by mail, no online version. It takes about 4–6 weeks to process. Free.

You can file it any time. There's no waiting period after EIN issuance. You could file it tomorrow if you wanted to get off Janice's address quickly — though if you don't have a PO Box yet, there's no urgency to file before you've actually set one up.

A USPS PO Box in Austin runs about $50–$100 every six months depending on size and location. They're available immediately if you walk into a post office with ID; can also be set up online at usps.com but you still have to go pick up the keys in person at the assigned post office. The smallest size is fine for institutional mail.

One thing to know: some banks will not accept a PO Box as the business address for account opening. They want a physical street address. So if you haven't opened the bank account yet, the order matters — open the bank account first (using whatever physical address you have available, even if it's still Janice's for now), then update everything to PO Box afterward via 8822-B for the IRS and a separate address change with the bank. Or use a CMRA (UPS Store, etc.) that gives you a real street-format address that satisfies the bank but functions like a PO Box otherwise.

The CMRA option is worth a second look given the constraints — for the same monthly cost as a PO Box, you get an address that satisfies banks, accepts packages (which a USPS PO Box won't reliably), and reads as a normal street address on every form you'll ever fill out. The UPS Store specifically does mail-forwarding and scanning if you want everything digital, which fits your "make everything end up on digital transmit" plan.

Current Relay terms, fresh as of today:

**The structural issue first.** Relay's nonprofit eligibility page says they support 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(6) entities specifically. They don't list 508(c)(1)(A) FBOs as a recognized category. That doesn't mean they'll reject you, but it does mean the application's "business type" dropdown probably won't have a clean fit for TMI. The closest match would be selecting "501(c)(3)" since the IRS treats 508(c)(1)(A) churches and church-equivalent organizations as automatically qualifying *as if they were* 501(c)(3) — they're exempt under the same general statutory framework, just without needing the determination letter. But that's a representation choice and you'd want to be consistent about it.

**The practical issue second.** Relay requires a physical U.S. business address — no PO boxes, no virtual mailboxes. If your legal business address is a registered agent, they want a second "operational business address" where activity actually happens, and that one also can't be a virtual mailbox or another RA. They specifically check this. For TMI right now, that's the Janice address or a similar real residential/commercial location. Hotel addresses are a gray area and they may flag.

**Fees and structure.** No monthly fee on the Starter plan. No minimum balance. No overdraft fees. Up to 20 individual checking accounts (useful for separating designated funds — housing allowance, operating, reserves, donor-restricted). Free incoming wires. Outgoing wires have a fee but it's lower than traditional banks. Debit card included. ACH transfers free. Banking services through Thread Bank (FDIC-insured up to $3M via sweep program).

**Application process.** Fully online. Estimated 10–15 minutes. Documents required:

- EIN (you have CP 575)
- Formation documents — for nonprofits this means bylaws, articles of incorporation if any, charter equivalent. Your signed bylaws + founding board resolution should satisfy this.
- Government-issued ID for the responsible party and any administrators
- Personal address for each person involved (must be physical U.S., no PO box) — this is your address, not TMI's
- Business address (physical, no PO box, no virtual mailbox)

How to Open a Bank Account for a 508(c)(1)(A) Organization

Open a bank account for your 508(c)(1)(A) organization. Navigate banking compliance when you lack the standard IRS determination letter.

The 508(c)(1)(A) designation grants automatic federal tax exemption to specific religious organizations, primarily churches and conventions of churches. This status means the organization does not need to file Form 1023, the formal application for recognition of exemption, with the Internal Revenue Service. The lack of a formal determination letter from the IRS, however, creates a specific friction point when attempting to establish a corporate bank account.

Financial institutions operate under strict Customer Identification Program (CIP) and Know Your Customer (KYC) regulations mandated by federal law. These regulations typically require a bank to verify an organization’s tax-exempt status using the official IRS determination letter. 

Failure to operate within the parameters of a church could result in the loss of the 508(c)(1)(A) status. This requires the organization to retroactively seek tax-exempt status through the standard Form 1023 process.

Preparing Required Documentation for Banking

The absence of an IRS Determination Letter makes the preparatory phase of documentation the single most important step in the banking process. The organization must construct a comprehensive file that fully satisfies the bank’s regulatory obligation to identify and verify the entity. This file must consist of four primary categories of documentation.

Organizational Documents

# How to Open a Bank Account for a 508(c)(1)(A) Organization

Open a bank account for your 508(c)(1)(A) organization. Navigate banking compliance when you lack the standard IRS determination letter.

[![](https://legalclarity.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/cropped-logoc.png)](https://legalclarity.org/users/8548/profile/legalclarity-team)

[LegalClarity Team](https://legalclarity.org/users/8548/profile/legalclarity-team)

Published Dec 9, 2025

The 508(c)(1)(A) designation grants automatic federal tax exemption to specific religious organizations, primarily churches and conventions of churches. This status means the organization does not need to file Form 1023, the formal application for recognition of exemption, with the Internal Revenue Service. The lack of a formal determination letter from the IRS, however, creates a specific friction point when attempting to establish a corporate bank account.

Financial institutions operate under strict Customer Identification Program (CIP) and Know Your Customer (KYC) regulations mandated by federal law. These regulations typically require a bank to verify an organization’s tax-exempt status using the official IRS determination letter. Since 508(c)(1)(A) organizations do not possess this standard letter, they must prepare an alternative package of documents to satisfy the bank’s compliance department.

This preparation requires a proactive approach centered on providing robust organizational documentation and a formal self-certification of the organization’s legal standing. Successfully opening the account depends entirely on the quality of these substituted documents and the organization’s ability to navigate the bank’s internal compliance review process.

## Understanding Automatic Tax Exempt Status

The legal foundation for the 508(c)(1)(A) designation is rooted in the automatic tax-exempt status granted to churches, conventions of churches, and integrated auxiliaries of a church. These entities are considered public charities under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code without any requirement to apply for the status. This automatic recognition is a significant benefit, bypassing the lengthy application process associated with Form 1023.

The IRS does not provide a single, all-encompassing definition of a “church” for tax purposes. Instead, the agency utilizes a cumulative list of criteria developed through case law. These criteria define the legal basis for the organization’s claim to 508(c)(1)(A) status.

The criteria used by the IRS to define a church generally include:

- Distinct legal existence and a recognized creed and form of worship.
- A formal code of doctrine and discipline.
- Membership not associated with any other church or denomination.
- Maintaining a regular congregation and established place of worship.
- The existence of ordained ministers and regular religious services.


The organization must meet these legal standards continuously to retain its automatic tax-exempt standing. Failure to operate within the parameters of a church could result in the loss of the 508(c)(1)(A) status. This requires the organization to retroactively seek tax-exempt status through the standard Form 1023 process.

## Preparing Required Documentation for Banking

The absence of an IRS Determination Letter makes the preparatory phase of documentation the single most important step in the banking process. The organization must construct a comprehensive file that fully satisfies the bank’s regulatory obligation to identify and verify the entity. This file must consist of four primary categories of documentation.

#### Organizational Documents

The bank requires sight of the documents that formally established the organization as a legal entity in its operating jurisdiction. This typically includes the Articles of Incorporation or a formal Trust Agreement filed with the relevant state authority. If the organization operates as an unincorporated association, the Constitution or a comprehensive set of Bylaws must be presented.

These documents establish the name of the entity, its purpose, and the structure of its governance. The bank will often require certified copies of these founding instruments.

#### Employer Identification Number (EIN) Confirmation

Every organization that intends to open a bank account or employ staff must possess an Employer Identification Number (EIN). The EIN is secured by filing Form SS-4 with the IRS, and the resulting confirmation letter serves as the official federal identification for the entity.

The bank needs this letter to confirm the organization’s name and its nine-digit federal tax identification number. It is a non-negotiable requirement for financial transactions and IRS reporting.

#### Organizational Resolution or Minutes

Banks require explicit authorization from the governing body to open an account and designate authorized signatories. This is accomplished through a formal document, such as a Board Resolution or a set of Meeting Minutes, signed by the trustees or directors.

The resolution must specifically name the bank, authorize the account opening, and clearly identify the individuals empowered to transact business. This includes naming authorized agents and specifying any transaction limits they are permitted to execute.

The bank will typically require an original, signed copy of this resolution to be kept on file.

#### Self-Certification of Status

Because the organization cannot provide a Form 1023 determination letter, it must provide a formal, notarized Self-Certification of its 508(c)(1)(A) status. This document is a written legal statement asserting that the organization meets all criteria for automatic tax exemption under the Internal Revenue Code.

The self-certification must explicitly state that the organization is a church, convention of churches, or integrated auxiliary of a church. It must assert that the organization meets all requirements to maintain its tax-exempt status.

This document acts as the organization’s declaration of compliance, serving as a substitute for the official IRS letter. The inclusion of a notary seal adds a layer of legal formality and authentication to the organization’s claim of status.

## Navigating the Bank Account Opening Process

Once all preparatory documentation has been assembled and formally executed, the organization is ready to approach the financial institution. This procedural step requires careful management of the bank’s internal processes and a prepared response to potential compliance friction.

Schedule a dedicated appointment with a bank officer who handles commercial or organizational accounts. Dealing with a teller is often insufficient, as specialized expertise is required. All authorized signatories named in the organizational resolution must be present at this appointment, bringing their government-issued identification.

The bank officer will initiate the formal Customer Identification Program process, verifying the identities of the signatories and reviewing the organizational documents. This review is where the 508(c)(1)(A) challenge typically arises.

Most bank personnel look for a standard IRS determination letter, and its absence triggers an internal flag. Present the Self-Certification and organizational documents as the alternative compliance package. Explain that the exemption from filing Form 1023 is explicitly permitted under Internal Revenue Code Section 508(c)(1)(A).

If the branch officer remains uncertain, the request must be escalated to the bank’s compliance department or legal counsel for a formal review. This escalation is a normal procedural hurdle for 508(c)(1)(A) organizations and should be anticipated.

The compliance review phase can take several days or even a few weeks, depending on the size and internal structure of the financial institution. During this period, the organization must remain available to provide any additional documentation or clarification requested. The process requires patience and persistence from the organization’s representatives.

Upon approval from the compliance department, the bank officer will finalize the account opening. Authorized individuals complete the required internal forms, including the signature card, the account agreement, and any necessary disclosures.

The account is officially established upon the completion of the paperwork and the deposit of the initial funding amount.

## Maintaining Compliance and Reporting Requirements

Successfully opening the bank account is the first step; long-term federal compliance requires adherence to specific reporting rules governing 508(c)(1)(A) entities. The primary benefit of this status is the general exemption from filing the annual information return, known as the Form 990 series.

The organization is not required to file Form 990, Form 990-EZ, or Form 990-N. This exemption significantly reduces the administrative burden associated with public disclosure and annual reporting requirements.

A significant exception involves Unrelated Business Taxable Income (UBTI). If the organization generates gross income of $1,000 or more from activities that constitute an unrelated trade or business, it must file Form 990-T.

Examples of UBTI include operating a bookstore selling items unrelated to the religious mission or renting property for commercial purposes. Form 990-T must be filed to report the taxable revenue.

The organization must also adhere to specific requirements if it engages in transactions with non-employees. Payments of $600 or more made to independent contractors or service providers during the calendar year require the organization to issue Form 1099-NEC. This requirement ensures that the IRS has a record of payments made for services rendered.

If the organization has employees, it must comply with all federal and state payroll tax withholding and reporting requirements. This includes filing quarterly Form 941 and annual Form W-2 for each employee. These payroll obligations are mandated regardless of the organization’s tax-exempt status.

Maintaining detailed financial records and internal accounting controls is paramount. These records must clearly differentiate between income from exempt activities and potential UBTI sources.

content.text:
Now I have a real picture. Here's the honest assessment of the landscape, no vendor spin.

**The structural problem first.** There is no list of banks that explicitly market themselves as "508(c)(1)(A) FBO friendly." The category is too small and too specific. What exists instead:

The friction point is universal. Banks operate under federal Customer Identification Program and Know Your Customer rules that require them to verify a nonprofit's tax-exempt status. The standard verification document is the IRS determination letter, which 508(c)(1)(A) FBOs don't have because they're exempt from applying for one. Every bank's compliance department has to make a judgment call when an FBO walks in without that letter. Some banks handle this routinely. Some don't.

The question isn't really "which banks serve 508(c)(1)(A) FBOs" — it's "which banks have compliance personnel who understand that not all churches have determination letters."

**Three categories of institution that handle this without friction:**

**Faith-aligned credit unions.** These exist because of the friction. Christian Community Credit Union (CCCU) and AdelFi merged December 2025 and are now the largest Christian credit union in the country. They explicitly serve "churches, ministries, and Christian-owned businesses" and are operationally familiar with the determination-letter gap. The catch: they require a faith statement / membership that's specifically Christian, and they're a credit union, so account opening involves a membership application process. Whether they accept TMI's specific theology as Christian-aligned would depend on review. Their statement of faith for membership is conservative evangelical Protestant. Reading TMI's bylaws and theological framework — Thessalonian work mandate, Proverbs 22:29 — that does fit the broad evangelical frame, but the specific theological framework PDF would need review against their membership requirements.

**Local Texas community banks and credit unions.** This is the path most small Texas churches actually use. A bank or CU within Austin that's processed church accounts before knows that a 508(c)(1)(A) FBO with bylaws + signed founding board resolution + CP 575 + a self-certification letter is a complete compliance package. The friction is the in-person visit, but the success rate is high because the staff has seen this before. Examples in Austin worth checking: Velocity Credit Union, University Federal Credit Union, Greater Texas Credit Union, A+ Federal Credit Union. Plus small local banks like Vista Bank, Texas Capital Bank, Frost Bank (Frost is large but Texas-based and known to handle religious nonprofits well). None of these will be online-only, but all have processed FBO accounts before.

**Fintech platforms.** Mercury, Relay, Bluevine, Novo. As we already discussed — these are designed for 501(c)(3) nonprofits with conventional structures. The application doesn't have a 508(c)(1)(A) category. They may approve TMI by routing it through "501(c)(3)" or "religious nonprofit" generic paths, or they may flag it for manual review and ask for documentation you don't have (determination letter, articles of incorporation if you didn't incorporate, etc.). It's a gamble. Pure online-only application but uncertain acceptance.

**The documentation package that actually unlocks any of these:**

The legalclarity article above identifies what banks specifically need from a 508(c)(1)(A) FBO when there's no determination letter. You already have most of it:

1. **Organizational documents** — bylaws (you have, signed) + articles of incorporation if you incorporated, OR the bylaws as a constitution-equivalent if you didn't. **Question for you:** did you file articles of incorporation with the Texas Secretary of State, or is TMI structured as an unincorporated faith-based organization? Your bylaws Section 1.2 calls TMI a "Faith-Based Organization" without specifying incorporation status. Banks will ask.

2. **EIN confirmation** — CP 575, you have it.

3. **Board resolution authorizing account opening** — Resolution 8 of your founding board resolution specifically authorizes this. You're covered.

4. **Self-certification letter on TMI letterhead** — this is the missing piece. A formal, notarized statement that TMI is a faith-based organization operating under 508(c)(1)(A) automatic exemption, signed by you as Minister, citing IRC § 508(c)(1)(A) and § 6033(a)(3)(A) by reference. Some banks accept it without notarization; some require it. Notarized is safer.

**My honest recommendation, given your specific constraints:**

The "fully online with no people interaction" path through the fintechs has real risk of decline or stall for an FBO without a determination letter. You can try it — it costs nothing — but plan for the possibility that it doesn't work.

The higher-probability path is one of two:

**Path A: CCCU/AdelFi.** Online application, faith-aligned, operationally familiar with determination-letter-free churches. Membership application process means there's some review and possibly an email exchange with their staff, but they do the church-account thing routinely. Worth investigating their current account-opening process for non-incorporated churches specifically.

**Path B: A local Austin credit union.** In-person visit required, but high acceptance probability. The "people interaction" piece is real, but it's a single bank officer in a routine appointment, not a phone call with the IRS. Configuration-wise: Minister-Jade walks in with a documented religious organization, hands over a complete compliance package, and the conversation is structured by their checklist. Not a free-form social interaction.

Want me to look up the specific account-opening process for CCCU/AdelFi for unincorporated faith-based organizations, or pull current information on a specific Austin credit union? Either is a worthwhile next step depending on which path is more tolerable.
