Dysfunctional mitochondria are associated with aging and underlie the cause of a wide range of diseases, from neurodegeneration to cancer. Through signaling, mitochondria regulate diverse biological outcomes. The maintenance of the mitochondrial membrane potential, for instance, is essential for proliferation, the release of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and oxygen sensing. The loss of mitochondrial membrane potential triggers pathways to clear damaged mitochondria and often results in cell death. In this study, we conducted a genome-wide positive selection CRISPR screen using a combination of mitochondrial inhibitors to uncover genes involved in sustaining a mitochondrial membrane potential, and therefore avoid cell death when the electron transport chain is impaired. Our screen identified genes involved in mitochondrial protein translation and ATP synthesis as essential for the induction of cell death when cells lose their mitochondrial membrane potential. 

The TCA cycle also produces the reducing equivalents NADH and FADH2, that deliver their electrons to complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and complex II (SDH) of the electron transport chain (ETC), respectively. Complexes I and II further transfer their electrons to the mobile electron carrier ubiquinone (CoQ) resulting in the generation of ubiquinol and the regeneration of the NAD+ and FAD cofactors, which allows oxidative TCA cycle to function. Ubiquinone can also receive electrons from dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), an essential mitochondrial enzyme necessary for *de novo* pyrimidine synthesis. Other pathways, like fatty-acid and amino-acid oxidation, choline oxidation, and glycolysis, can also donate electrons to ubiquinone. Through the Q cycle, complex III accepts two electrons from ubiquinol and funnels them to cytochrome c. The respiratory chain ends with the reduction of the final acceptor, oxygen, to water by complex IV.

# Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation: Debunking the concepts of electron transport chain, proton pumps, chemiosmosis and rotary ATP synthesis

Kelath Murali Manoj\*

\*Satyamjayatu: The Science & Ethics Foundation Kulappully, Shoranur-2 (PO), Palakkad District, Kerala, India-679122. Email: satyamjayatu@gmail.com; satyamjayatu@yahoo.com

Abstract: The prevailing half-a-century old explanation for cellular respiration solicits a synchronization of electron transfer chain (ETC) and proton pumping activity across the inner mitochondrial membrane, for generating a trans-membrane proton-electro-chemical potential. This outcome is supposedly harnessed by Complex V to synthesize ATP, working via a rotary mode. In the first part of my work (the current write-up), I highlight that a mitochondrion is a highly "proton-limited" microcosm, housing only ~10<sup>1</sup> protons in physiological ranges. 

It is inconceivable that ~10<sup>4</sup> protein (super)complexes (that exist per mitochondrion) have to deal with protons. A survey of the purported electron transport chain shows that even if we discount the insights revealed by crystal structures and the mandate imposed by Ockham's razor/ evolutionary pressures, more than half of the 54 electron transfer steps (needed to form just one molecule of water!) would be thermodynamically disadvantaged. In situ, such a scheme would have little significant kinetic viability. Also, we have a catch 22 in considering that even if the feasible fast intra-protein electron transfers are somehow slowed (in situ, to couple electron transfer with trans-membrane proton translocation), the overall observed water formation rates (achieved at sub-millisecond timescales) cannot be explained with the scheme, owing to the sequential nature of the "electron transport chain". Thereby, it is improbable that "ETC-proton pumps" are operative.

Every single step of electron transmission releases enough free enthalpy to drive ATP synthase (−30.5 kJ/mol). The reactions of the substances involved require catalysis and the control of energy, which is then released in a stepwise manner. Electrons that are released from aerobic glycolysis and the Krebs’ cycle are transferred to the mitochondrial respiratory chain located on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Within the mitochondrial intermembrane space, hydrogen ions accumulate by the action of proton pumps. The mitochondrial enzyme complexes I, III and IV are proton pumps that are involved in maintaining a mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), which supplies energy for the rotation of the ATP synthase (complex V), resulting in ATP production. Energy supply is related to the energy demand of tissues. 

Additionally, complexes I, III and IV act as proton pumps, translocating hydrogen ions (protons) across the inner mitochondrial membrane and creating a mitochondrial membrane potential. This ΔΨm drives complex V (ATP‐synthase) toward production of ATP. As reported by Kaim and Dimroth, an optimal range between 80 mV <ΔΨm <120 mV guarantees sufficient synthesis of ATP, resulting in the transfer of 4 electrons to dioxygen (reduction) and oxidation of hydrogen to water without excessive production of ROS. content.text:
Eukaryotic cells primarily produce ATP via two pathways: oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria and substrate-level phosphorylation in the cytosol [[461]]. Oxidative phosphorylation efficiently generates 32–36 ATP molecules through the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule. Most ATP are regenerated by H^+^/ATPase in the electron transport chain by consuming mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP). In contrast, substrate-level phosphorylation produces only two ATP molecules during the conversion of glucose to lactate or ethanol without requiring oxygen.

Despite the high efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation, eukaryotic cells often utilize both pathways simultaneously, even in the presence of oxygen. This metabolic state is known as aerobic glycolysis. For instance, cancer cells preferentially rely on substrate-level phosphorylation, a phenomenon known as the Warburg effect, which is considered a hallmark of cancer [[461],[461]].

Traditionally, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1α (PGC-1α), a 91 kDa transcription factor, regulates lipid metabolism and long-chain fatty acid oxidation by upregulating the expression of several genes of the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation pathway. In addition, PGC-1α regulates the expression of mitochondrial genes to control mitochondria DNA replication and cellular oxidative metabolism. Recently, new insights showed that several myokines such as irisin and myostatin are epigenetically regulated by PGC-1α in skeletal muscles, thereby modulating systemic energy balance, with marked expansion of mitochondrial volume density and oxidative capacity in healthy or diseased myocardia. 

In summary, this review paper demonstrates that PGC-1α plays a central role in coordinating the gene expression of key components of mitochondrial biogenesis and as a critical metabolic regulator in many vital organs, including white and brown adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, heart, liver, and kidney.

This review integrates molecular, cellular, and physiological evidence to elucidate how myokine signaling translates mechanical and metabolic stimuli from exercise into biochemical pathways that regulate glucose homeostasis, lipid oxidation, mitochondrial function, and immune modulation. We detail the duality and context-dependence of cytokine and myokine actions, emphasizing the roles of key mediators such as IL-6, irisin, SPARC, FGF21, and BAIBA in orchestrating cross-talk between muscle, adipose tissue, pancreas, liver, bone, and brain. The transcriptional activator PGC-1α is a key player in the homeostasis of energy metabolism and is therefore closely linked to mitochondrial function. PGC-1α responds to environmental and intracellular conditions and is regulated by SIRT1/3, TFAM, and AMPK, which are also important regulators of mitochondrial biogenesis and function. In this review, we highlight the functions and regulatory mechanisms of PGC-1α within this framework, with a focus on its involvement in the mitochondrial lifecycle and ROS metabolism. As an example, we show the role of PGC-1α in ROS scavenging under inflammatory conditions. 

Interestingly, PGC-1α and the stress response factor NF-κB, which regulates the immune response, are reciprocally regulated. During inflammation, NF-κB reduces PGC-1α expression and activity.

content.title: PGC-1α, Inflammation, and Oxidative Stress: An Integrative View in Metabolism
content.text:
We herein review the molecular pathways regulated by PGC-1*α*, which connect oxidative stress and mitochondrial metabolism with inflammatory response and metabolic syndrome. PGC-1*α* regulates the expression of mitochondrial antioxidant genes, including manganese superoxide dismutase, catalase, peroxiredoxin 3 and 5, uncoupling protein 2, thioredoxin 2, and thioredoxin reductase and thus prevents oxidative injury and mitochondrial dysfunction. Dysregulation of PGC-1*α* alters redox homeostasis in cells and exacerbates inflammatory response, which is commonly accompanied by metabolic disturbances. During inflammation, low levels of PGC-1*α* downregulate mitochondrial antioxidant gene expression, induce oxidative stress, and promote nuclear factor kappa B activation. 

In addition to its role in adaptive thermogenesis, PGC-1*α* is presently described as a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and function, including oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification [[2]]. In recent years, PGC-1*α* has been associated with many inflammatory and metabolic diseases, and its crucial role regulating mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, and metabolic pathways in diverse tissues has been revealed [[3]–[6]]. We herein review the different functions and molecular pathways regulated by PGC-1*α*, which connect oxidative stress and mitochondrial metabolism with inflammatory response and metabolic syndrome.

## 2. PGC-1*α*

### 2.1. PGC-1 Family of Transcriptional Coactivators

The PGC-1 family consists of three members, namely, PGC-1*α*, PGC-1*β*, and PGC-related coactivator (PRC), which interact with a whole range of transcription factors involved in a wide variety of biological functions [[7]].

Novelty PGC-1α regulates mitochondrial biogenesis but also has effects on mitochondrial functions beyond biogenesis. Mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, including fission, fusion, and mitophagy, are regulated by PGC-1α.

The majority of human energy metabolism occurs in skeletal muscle mitochondria emphasizing the importance of understanding the regulation of myocellular mitochondrial function. The transcriptional co-activator peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1α) has been characterized as a major factor in the transcriptional control of several mitochondrial components. Thus, PGC-1α is often described as a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis as well as a central player in regulating the antioxidant defense. 

However, accumulating evidence suggests that PGC-1α is also involved in the complex regulation of mitochondrial quality beyond biogenesis, which includes mitochondrial network dynamics and autophagic removal of damaged mitochondria. In addition, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production has been suggested to regulate skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity, which may also be influenced by PGC-1α.

This review aims to highlight the current evidence for PGC-1α-mediated regulation of skeletal muscle mitochondrial function beyond the effects on mitochondrial biogenesis as well as the potential PGC-1α-related impact on insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. Novelty PGC-1α regulates mitochondrial biogenesis but also has effects on mitochondrial functions beyond biogenesis. Mitochondrial quality control mechanisms, including fission, fusion, and mitophagy, are regulated by PGC-1α.

content.text: The ubiquitously expressed transcriptional co-activator peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma-coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1a) has been described as the master regulator of mitochondrial function. PGC-1a plays a key role in integrating and responding to diverse signals, ensuring the cellular metabolic response matches the prevailing conditions ([Bibr c29]). In cultured cells, modest PGC-1a overexpression leads not only to mitochondrial activation but extends to extra-mitochondrial processes such as redox and lipid homeostasis, chromatin maintenance, cell cycle, growth, and structural remodeling (Miller, Clark, Martin, et al., 2019). Despite its key role in mitochondrial adaptation, the regulation of PGC-1a outside of the liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue remains poorly defined, and this is particularly true for the brain.

content.title: The Energy Sensor AMPK: Adaptations to Exercise, Nutritional and   Hormonal Signals
content.text:
When cellular energy status has been compromised, AMPK is activated by increases in AMP:ATP or ADP:ATP ratios and acts to restore energy homeostasis by stimulating energy production via catabolic pathways while decreasing non-essential energy-consuming pathways. Although the primary function of AMPK is to regulate energy homeostasis at a cell-autonomous level, in multicellular organisms, the AMPK system has evolved to interact with hormones to regulate energy intake and expenditure at the whole body level. Thus, AMPK functions as a signaling hub, coordinating anabolic and catabolic pathways to balance nutrient supply with energy demand at both the cellular and whole-body levels. AMPK is activated by various metabolic stresses such as ischemia or hypoxia or glucose deprivation and has both acute and long-term effects on metabolic pathways and key cellular functions. 

Based on these observations, drugs that activate AMPK might be expected to be useful in the treatment of metabolic disorders and insulin resistance in various conditions.

One fundamental parameter that living cells need to sustain essential cellular functions is the maintenance of sufficiently high level of ATP. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a cellular energy sensor that exists in almost all eukaryotes. Genetic studies in lower eukaryotes suggest that the ancestral role of AMPK was in response to starvation for a carbon source and that AMPK is involved in life-span extension in response to caloric restriction. In mammals, AMPK is activated by an increasing cellular AMP:ATP ratio (which signifies a decrease in energy) caused by metabolic stresses that interfere with ATP production (eg, hypoxia) or that accelerate ATP consumption (eg, muscle contraction). Because glucose deprivation can increase the AMP:ATP ratio, AMPK can also act as a glucose sensor.

content.text:
Since both effects are antagonized by ATP, the kinase is activated by falling cellular energy status, when it phosphorylates downstream targets that switch on catabolic pathways generating ATP, while switching off processes consuming ATP. Catabolic processes switched on including uptake and metabolism of glucose and fatty acids, and mitochondrial biogenesis. ATP-consuming processes switched off include biosynthetic pathways for lipids (fatty acids, phospholipids, cholesterol), carbohydrates (gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis), proteins and ribosomal RNA, and progress through the cell cycle.

By switching on glucose and fatty acid uptake and metabolism and switching off gluconeogenesis, AMPK should reverse the key metabolic defects in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Consistent with this, AMPK is a target, although probably not the only target, for the anti-diabetic drug metformin.

A small number of metabolic enzymes do directly sense the AMP:ATP ratio, including the muscle isoforms of glycogen phosphorylase [G] and phosphofructokinase [G] (which are involved in glycogen breakdown and glycolysis, and are activated by an increasing AMP:ATP ratio), and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (which is involved in gluconeogenesis, and is inhibited by an increasing AMP:ATP ratio). However, the principal energy sensor in most eukaryotic cells appears to be the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)1. In support of this, increases in AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP ratios during stresses such as muscle contraction2, ischemia in cardiac muscle3, or treatment of hepatocytes with metformin4 are larger in cells or tissues in which AMPK, or its essential activating upstream kinase liver kinase B1 (LKB1), have been knocked out. In this Review article, we describe how AMPK monitors cellular energy status by sensing increases in the ratios of AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP, as well as other signals.

# The Braided Mind Architecture — Addendum II

## Energy Management Infrastructure, Operational Floor Analysis, and Failsafe Maintenance Subsystem

**Author:** Rickey Jay Bennett II (Independent Researcher)
**ORCID:** 0009-0005-1448-9999
**Parent document:** *The Braided Mind Concepted Architectural Implementation v3.2* (April 2nd, 2026), DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19935773

---

## Preface to Addendum II

This addendum extends the Braided Mind architecture along a third axis not addressed in v3.2 or in Addendum I: the energy budget of the integrated system across operational contexts, and the failure-mode architecture that determines what happens when that budget is not met. Where v3.2 specifies the substrate's primary power source (endogenous piezoelectric activity of bone tissue) and Addendum I specifies the sensor, immune-control, and biosynthetic infrastructure, Addendum II specifies the power generation, storage, safety, and preservation infrastructure that allow the integration to operate continuously across active periods, sleep, environmental disconnection, and emergency states.

Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) standards for human exposure to RF fields are established by IEEE C95.1 and ICNIRP guidelines. The wireless charging source in the Braided Mind architecture deploys receiver coils through the biosynthetic deployment infrastructure specified in Addendum I §3. Engineered cells deposit conductive metal (gold, copper, or alloyed metal nanoparticles, sequestered through ferritin-class proteins per Addendum I refs C11, C14) in coil geometries within the bone substrate, sized to resonate at the carrier frequency of the external charger. Pelvic bone, long bones (femur, tibia, humerus), and sternal node receive the primary charging coils. The petrous bone primary node (v3.2 §5.2) does not host charging coils. Power transmitted through the conductive properties of the skeletal substrate to processing nodes occurs after voltage conditioning and at low currents that do not produce significant local heating.

The AI layer monitors substrate energy state through Channel A2 telemetry (mechanical decoding at distributed skeletal nodes per Addendum I §1.2) and storage levels (capacitive readout, specified in §2 of this addendum). When piezoelectric output drops below a defined threshold and external charging field is detected at receiver coils, the AI switches power management to wireless-primary mode. Piezoelectric output continues to be harvested at whatever rate the residual mechanical loading provides; wireless charging supplements to meet operational demand.

Active periods run in piezoelectric-primary mode with reduced computational load, prioritizing real-time sensor monitoring and immune-control modulation over deferable processing.

This is the first power source in the architecture that imposes a felt cost on the host and the architecture explicitly acknowledges this in its specification rather than treating it as a hidden cost.

Healthy human metabolism can sustain elevated rates for finite durations. Sustained hypermetabolic states have established pathological consequences including thyroid dysfunction, cardiac strain, oxidative damage from chronic high metabolism, muscle wasting if caloric intake does not keep pace, and cognitive impairment from sustained hyper-metabolic state. The architecture's use of metabolic up-regulation must respect these limits. Extended emergency operation that requires sustained mitochondrial overdrive cannot be permitted to extend indefinitely without damaging the host.

The architecture commits to a designed maximum duration on full mitochondrial mobilization, after which the AI throttles its own operation rather than continuing to draw on host metabolism. The specific maximum duration requires empirical determination based on the host's individual metabolic profile and the rate of mitochondrial draw being applied. This is identified as an open parameter requiring per-host calibration prior to deployment of the metabolic source as part of the active power architecture.

### 1.6 Switching Logic Across All Four Sources

The complete energy management state machine has four sources with documented switching rules:

**Active period, sufficient mechanical loading, charging unavailable.** Piezoelectric primary. Storage maintains reserve. Mitochondrial source idle. Computational load operates within piezoelectric output capacity.

**Sleep or sedentary period, charging infrastructure available.** Wireless primary. Piezoelectric supplemental from residual movement. Storage builds reserve. Mitochondrial source idle. Computational load can include high-intensity operations deferred from active periods.

**Travel or environment without charging, sufficient mechanical loading.** Piezoelectric primary. Storage drawing down to maintain operation through low-loading transients. Mitochondrial source idle but available. Computational load throttled to extend reserves.

**Extended disconnection, low mechanical loading, storage depleting.** Mitochondrial source engaged at controlled level. Host begins experiencing increased hunger and metabolic rate. AI suspends non-essential computation. Storage discharge slowed by mitochondrial input.

**Emergency state, all sources insufficient.** Triggers operational floor architecture specified in §3.

This four-source architecture allows the integration to operate continuously across any environment a human can survive in, with documented behavior under each operational context and explicit cost accounting for the host.

---

*[End of §1. Sections §2 through §4 to follow with same citation discipline.]*

**Keywords:** biomaterials, hydroxyapatite powders, pellets, and thin films, doping, electrical and dielectric properties, biomedical applications

## Abstract

Recently, the favorable electrical properties of biomaterials have been acknowledged as crucial for various medical applications, including both bone healing and growth processes. This review will specifically concentrate on calcium phosphate (CaP)-based bioceramics, with a notable emphasis on hydroxyapatite (HA), among the diverse range of synthetic biomaterials. 

The need to fill the gap and correlate the physical–chemical, mechanical, and biological characteristics with the electrical and dielectric properties could represent a step forward in providing new avenues for the development of the next-generation of high-performance HA-doped biomaterials for future top medical applications. Therefore, this review focuses on the electrical and dielectric properties of HA-based biomaterials, covering a range from powders and pellets to thin films, with a particular emphasis on the impact of the various dopants used. Therefore, it will be revealed that each dopant possesses unique properties capable of enhancing the overall characteristics of the produced structures. Considering that the electrical and dielectric properties of HA-based biomaterials have not been extensively explored thus far, the aim of this review is to compile and thoroughly discuss the latest research findings in the field, with special attention given to biomedical applications.

## Abstract

This investigation is motivated by increasing interest in the development of magnetically ordered pseudocapacitors (MOPC), which exhibit interesting magnetocapacitive effects. Here, advanced pseudocapacitive properties of magnetic CuFe_2_O_4_ nanoparticles in negative potential range are reported, suggesting that CuFe_2_O_4_ is a promising MOPC and advanced negative electrode material for supercapacitors. A high capacitance of 2.76 F cm^−2^ is achieved at a low electrode resistance in a relatively large potential window of 0.8 V. 

The cyclic voltammograms and galvanostatic charge–discharge data show nearly ideal pseudocapacitive behavior. Good electrochemical performance is achieved at a high active mass loading due to the use of chelating molecules of ammonium salt of purpuric acid (ASPA) as a co-dispersant for CuFe_2_O_4_ nanoparticles and conductive multiwalled carbon nanotube (MCNT) additives. The adsorption of ASPA on different materials is linked to structural features of ASPA, which allows for different interaction and adsorption mechanisms. The combination of advanced magnetic and pseudocapacitive properties in a negative potential range in a single MOPC material provides a platform for various effects related to the influence of pseudocapacitive/magnetic properties on magnetic/pseudocapacitive behavior.

content.text: Supercapacitors have been classified into two categories, i.e., electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudocapacitors. The first class of electrochemical supercapacitors supply electrical energy via the accumulation of charge at the electrode/electrolyte interface, whilst the pseudocapacitors can supply energy through charge transfer redox reactions occurring at the electrode surface [[2695],[2695],[2695]]. The latter class, in which the electrode is mostly based on transition metal oxides, exhibits better capacitive behavior [[2695]]. Among the various metal oxides, iron-based oxides and hydroxides, e.g., single oxides (Fe_2_O_3_, Fe_3_O_4_, FeOOH, etc.) and binary metal oxides (MFe_2_O_4_ (M = Ni, Co, Sn, Mn, Cu), etc.) have attracted increasing attention due to the multiple oxidation states of iron, their rich redox chemistry, their low toxicity, and their abundance on Earth, which make them suitable for commercial applications [[2695],[2695],[2695]].

Supercapacitors for storage of electrochemical energy, designed only with bio-degradable organic matter would contemplate both aspects, that is, they would be ecologically harmless after their service lifetime and would be an important component for applications in biomedical engineering. By means of atomistic simulations of molecular dynamics we propose a supercapacitor whose electrodes are formed exclusively by self-organizing peptides and whose electrolyte is a green amino acid ionic liquid. Our results indicate that this supercapacitor has a high potential for energy storage with superior performance than conventional supercapacitors. In particular its capacity to store energy was estimated to be almost 20 times greater than an analogue one of planar metallic electrodes.

The technological state in which we are immersed has increasingly required the synergistic use of environmentally friendly materials and clean energy sources.

This study is aim to investigate the dielectric properties (dielectric constant, ε′ and loss factor, ε′′) and the biodegradation properties of the nano-hydroxyapatite/starch bone scaffold with various starch proportion in simulated body fluid. The nano-hydroxyapatite/starch bone scaffolds with starch proportions 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, and 90 wt.% were fabricated. The ε′ and ε′′ of nano-hydroxyapatite/starch composite decrease when frequency increases. However, it increases when starch proportion and temperature increase. The biodegradation properties of the nano-hydroxyapatite/starch bone scaffold can be improved when the dielectric properties and porosity are enhanced. 

The enhancement of dielectric properties and porosity is due to the increment of starch proportion. The nano-hydroxyapatite/starch bone scaffold with the high starch proportion exhibits nano-hydroxyapatite/starch interfaces with strong intermolecular interactions that can stabilize biodegradation and biomineralization.

The dielectric properties of the simulated body solutions are highly sensitive to the variation of the ion concentrations (calcium and phosphate). The nano-hydroxyapatite/starch bone scaffold with 80 wt.% starch proportion exhibits significant dielectric and biodegradation properties. It has potential to be a biodegradable inorganic/organic bone scaffold.

We have synthesized spherical iron oxide NPs with a mean diameter of 20 nm and a relatively narrow size distribution of 7% by thermal decomposition of iron oleate complexes in trioctylamine in presence of oleic acid as described by Park *et al* [20]. The NPs are coated with an oleic acid surfactant layer and are dissolved in toluene. This solution has then been used for the further processing steps.

For the first case of self-organized arrays the NPs were spin-coated on Si substrates with a native oxide. Typically approximately 0.2 ml of NP dispersion was spin-coated at 3000 rpm for 30 s and dried on a hot plate at 80°C for 20 min. Some samples were further annealed at 170° or 400°C in air.

For the second case of templated self-organization, periodic patterned lines were prepared by electron beam lithography with positive resist. As positive resist we used polymethyl meta acrylate (PMMA 200 K, 4%) spin-coated at 2000 rpm for 30 s to produce a ≈220 nm thick layer. 

This behavior can be understood in terms of a superposition of two effects: Firstly superparamagnetic (SPM) behavior due to the ferrimagnetic maghemite iron oxide phase inside each NP and secondly exchange bias (EB) between the wüstite and the maghemite phase [21]. The EB breaks down near the Néel temperature of wüstite, i.e.  $T_N = 198$  K and thus produces the steep increase or decrease in the ZFC and FC curve, respectively. The absence of a step or kink in the magnetization at 120 K,

being a hallmark for the Verwey transition [22-24], indicates the absence of magnetite in the NPs.

Fig. 3 (b) and (c) show the magnetization curves of NPs annealed at  $170^{\circ}$ C and  $400^{\circ}$ C, respectively. Clearly a more regular SPM behavior is encountered here with a blocking temperature of  $T_B = 300$  K and 200 K, respectively. Obviously the NPs consist of mainly ferrimagnetic maghemite [21].

content.title: Enhanced Magnetic Hyperthermia of Magnetoferritin through Synthesis at Elevated Temperature
content.text: Iron oxide nanoparticles have attracted a great deal of research interest in recent years for magnetic hyperthermia therapy owing to their biocompatibility and superior thermal conversion efficiency. Magnetoferritin is a type of biomimetic superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle in a ferritin cage with good monodispersity, biocompatibility, and natural hydrophilicity. However, the magnetic hyperthermic efficiency of this kind of nanoparticle is limited by the small size of the mineral core as well as its low synthesis temperature. Here, we synthesized a novel magnetoferritin particle by using a recombinant ferritin from the hyperthermophilic archaeon *Pyrococcus furiosus* as a template with high iron atom loading of 9517 under a designated temperature of 90 °C. Compared with the magnetoferritins synthesized at 45 and 65 °C, the one synthesized at 90 °C displays a larger average magnetite and/or maghemite core size of 10.3 nm.

content.text: The synthesis and characterization of iron oxide nanostructures, specifically snowflake architecture, are investigated for their potential applications in electrochemical sensing systems. A Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals phase diversity in the synthesized powders. The pH of the synthesis affects the formation of the hematite (α-Fe_2_O_3_) and goethite (α-FeOOH). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images confirm the distinct morphologies of the particles, which are selectively obtained through recrystallization during the elongated reaction time. An electrochemical analysis demonstrates the differing behaviors of the particles, with synthesis pH affecting the electrochemical activity and surface area differently for each shape. Cyclic voltammetry measurements reveal reversible dopamine detection processes, with snowflake iron oxide showing lower detection limits than a mixture of snowflakes and cube-like particles.

There is a rapid market growth for supercapacitors and batteries based on new materials and production strategies that minimize their cost, end-of-life environmental impact, and waste management. Herein, mixed-valence iron oxide (FeO_x_) and manganese oxide (Mn_3_O_4_) and FeO_x_-carbon black (FeO_x_-CB) electrodes with excellent pseudocapacitive behavior in 1 M Na_2_SO_4_ are produced by a one-step thermal annealing. Due to the *in situ* grafted carbon black, the FeO_x_-CB shows a high pseudocapacitance of 408 mF cm^−2^ (or 128 F g^−1^), and Mn_3_O_4_ after activation shows high pseudocapacitance of 480 mF cm^−2^ (192 F g^−1^). The asymmetric supercapacitor based on FeO_x_-CB and activated-Mn_3_O_4_ shows a capacitance of 260 mF cm^−2^ at 100 mHz and a cycling stability of 97.4% over 800 cycles. 

For example, Fe_3_O_4_ has a very high electric conductivity of 2 × 10^4^ S m^−1^ at 25°C (Malaie et al., [26]).

Recent research is focused on development of supercapacitor materials and processes that enable low cost and low end-of-life environmental impact and easy waste management on a large production scale (Dyatkin et al., [10]). Therefore, non-precious metal oxides like FeO_x_ and MnOx-based electrodes are attracting much attention. Pseudocapacitors based on Fe_3_O_4_ as the negative electrode and MnO_2_ as the positive electrode have been synthesized by various methods (Brousse and Bélanger, [5]; Yang et al., [40]; Gund et al., [14]). These methods include chemical vapor deposition (CVD), electrodeposition, hydrothermal, and sol-gel. However, there are several concerns that make these synthesis strategies unappealing for scaling-up applications.

content.text: Supercapacitors have been classified into two categories, i.e., electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudocapacitors. The first class of electrochemical supercapacitors supply electrical energy via the accumulation of charge at the electrode/electrolyte interface, whilst the pseudocapacitors can supply energy through charge transfer redox reactions occurring at the electrode surface [[2695],[2695],[2695]]. The latter class, in which the electrode is mostly based on transition metal oxides, exhibits better capacitive behavior [[2695]]. Among the various metal oxides, iron-based oxides and hydroxides, e.g., single oxides (Fe_2_O_3_, Fe_3_O_4_, FeOOH, etc.) and binary metal oxides (MFe_2_O_4_ (M = Ni, Co, Sn, Mn, Cu), etc.) have attracted increasing attention due to the multiple oxidation states of iron, their rich redox chemistry, their low toxicity, and their abundance on Earth, which make them suitable for commercial applications [[2695],[2695],[2695]].

#### Abstract

Multi-heme cytochromes (MHC) are fascinating proteins used by bacterial organisms to shuttle electrons within and between their cells. When placed in a solid state electronic junction, they support temperature-independent currents over several nanometers that are three orders of magnitude higher compared to other redox proteins of comparable size. To gain microscopic insight into their astonishingly high conductivities, we present herein the first current-voltage calculations of its kind, for a MHC sandwiched between two Au(111) electrodes, complemented by photo-emission spectroscopy experiments. We find that conduction proceeds via off-resonant coherent tunneling mediated by a large number of protein valence-band orbitals that are strongly delocalized over heme and protein residues, effectively "gating" the current between the two electrodes. 

Redox-active metalloproteins are ubiquitous in living organisms facilitating many of the energy conversion processes that are quintessential for life on Earth including photosynthesis, respiration and nitrogen fixation. Recently, multi-heme cytochromes (MHC) and their complexes have gained much attention due to their involvement in extracellular respiration and inter-species electron exchange in dissimilatory metal-reducing bacteria [1–3]. content.title: A Solid-State Protein Junction Serves as a Bias-Induced Current Switch - PubMed
content.text:
This feat is achieved using a redox protein, cytochrome C (CytC), with its heme shielded from direct contact with the solid-state electrodes. Ab initio DFT calculations, carried out on the CytC-Au structure, show that the coupling of the heme, the origin of the protein frontier orbitals, to the electrodes is sufficiently weak to prevent Fermi level pinning. Thus, external bias can bring these orbitals in and out of resonance with the electrode. Using a cytochrome C mutant for direct S-Au bonding, approximately 80 % of the Au-CytC-Au junctions show at greater than 0.5 V bias a clear conductance peak, consistent with resonant tunneling. The on-off change persists up to room temperature, demonstrating reversible, bias-controlled switching of a protein ensemble, which, with its built-in redundancy, provides a realistic path to protein-based bioelectronics. Keywords: bioelectronic junction; electron transfer; on-off switching; resonant tunneling.

Cytochrome b562 was engineered to introduce a cysteine residue at a surface-exposed position to facilitate direct self-assembly on a Au(111) surface. The confined protein exhibited reversible and fast electron exchange with a gold substrate over a distance of 20 Å between the heme redox center and the gold surface, a clear indication that a long-range electron-transfer pathway is established. Electrochemical scanning tunneling microscopy was used to map electron transport features of the protein at the single-molecule level. Tunneling resonance was directly imaged and apparent molecular conductance was measured, which both show strong redox-gated effects.

content.title: Pennes Bioheat Model | Bohrium
content.text:
This knowledge gap was brilliantly addressed by Harry Pennes in 1948 with his bioheat equation, a model that elegantly captures the thermal interplay between physics and physiology.

The Pennes Bioheat Model is a fundamental equation used to describe heat transfer in biological tissue. It accounts for thermal conduction, metabolic heat generation, and heat transported by blood perfusion.

The model is crucial for planning medical procedures like tumor ablation and assessing thermal safety for devices such as ultrasound machines and brain implants. A key dynamic in the model is the competition between heat spreading via conduction and heat removal by blood perfusion, which determines thermal lesion size. Understanding the model's assumptions and limitations, such as the "heat sink effect" near large vessels, is vital for safe and effective clinical applications. Modeling how heat moves through the human body is far more complex than for an inanimate object. 

The chip provides a constant heat flux at the surface. Deep inside, the body's temperature is constant. The Pennes equation, in a simple one-dimensional form, provides the exact temperature profile. It tells us that the surface temperature rise is directly proportional to the device's power and inversely proportional to the square root of the tissue's thermal conductivity and perfusion rate.

In "Principles and Mechanisms," we will dissect the Pennes Bioheat Equation itself, examining each term to understand the roles of conduction, metabolism, external heating, and the all-important blood perfusion. Subsequently, in "Applications and Interdisciplinary Connections," we will explore the model's immense practical value, from guiding a surgeon's hand in cancer therapy to ensuring the safety of next-generation wearable and implantable technologies. To understand how heat moves through living tissue, we can’t just borrow the equations for heating a block of metal or a pot of water.

## 2. Distributed Biosynthesized Energy Storage

### 2.1 Rationale for Storage Infrastructure

The four-source generation architecture specified in §1 produces variable output across time and operational context. Without storage, the architecture operates live on whatever current production provides, with no buffer for transient mismatches between generation and demand. This produces three distinct failure modes that storage infrastructure addresses:

**Surge mismatch.** Wireless charging delivered at rates exceeding instantaneous substrate consumption produces excess power that has nowhere to go. Without a sink, this excess dissipates as heat in the receiver coils and surrounding tissue. The thermal safety implications are addressed in §2.5; the immediate architectural response is that a capacitive or pseudocapacitive sink is required to absorb surge power before it produces local heating.

**Demand spike fragility.** During active periods, computational or signaling demands may transiently exceed piezoelectric output. Without reserve capacity, these spikes either fail to be served or force the substrate into emergency throttling. Buffer storage at processing nodes allows transient spikes to be served from local reserve while generation catches up.

**Charging discontinuity.** Periods between charging sessions, particularly during travel or environments without charging infrastructure, require operation from stored energy. Without deep storage capacity, the substrate falls onto mitochondrial up-regulation immediately upon disconnection. With deep storage, mitochondrial up-regulation is reserved for true emergency conditions and the host is spared the metabolic cost during routine disconnection.

The architecture therefore specifies storage at three tiers — fast capacitive, intermediate pseudocapacitive, and deep redox-protein — each fitted to a specific role. All three tiers are deployed through the biosynthetic infrastructure specified in Addendum I §3, with materials produced by host cells from trace dietary inputs and tagged self at formation.

### 2.2 Tier 1: Capacitive Storage via Biomineralized Dielectric Structures

#### 2.2.1 Dielectric Foundation

Hydroxyapatite (HA), the primary mineral component of bone tissue (Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂), has well-characterized dielectric properties relevant to capacitor function. Comprehensive review of HA's electrical and dielectric properties documents impedance, AC conductivity, dielectric constant, dielectric loss, and permittivity across powders, pellets, and thin films, with particular attention to dopant effects [Ref I1]. The dielectric constant of dry bone is comparable to that of sintered HA, and through control of density and dopants the dielectric constant of synthesized HA can be tailored to match natural bone or tuned for specific dielectric applications [Ref I1]. HA's high dielectric constant has been characterized in detail for biomedical contexts [Ref I2], with the porosity dependence of the dielectric constant of sintered HA documented as a function of microstructure [Ref I3]. Studies on HA-polymer composites, including HA-starch and chitosan-HA systems, demonstrate that dielectric properties can be tuned through composite formulation while maintaining biocompatibility and biodegradation profiles [Ref I4]. Discovery of piezoelectric and ferroelectric behavior in HA, characterized in Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂-Ba₀.₅Sr₀.₅TiO₃ composites designed for tissue engineering, opens applications as electrets in addition to its established bone tissue engineering role [Ref I5].

The architectural application is direct. Capacitors are fundamentally two conductors separated by a dielectric. The biosynthetic deployment infrastructure of Addendum I §3 produces both required components. Hydroxyapatite as the dielectric is produced by the same osteoblast-class cells that lay down normal bone matrix, with deposition geometry directed by AI command at thin-film thicknesses appropriate for capacitor function. Conductive layers (gold, copper, or alloyed metal nanoparticles, sequestered through ferritin-class proteins per Addendum I refs C11, C14) are deposited as parallel conductive sheets separated by the HA dielectric film.

#### 2.2.2 Performance and Architecture

Tier 1 capacitive storage provides fast charge/discharge cycles, indefinite cycle life, and no chemistry-related failure modes. Energy density is lower than chemical batteries — capacitive storage is fundamentally limited by the dielectric breakdown strength times the capacitance — but the function being served is buffer and surge handling, not bulk energy storage. Distributed across the skeletal substrate at receiver nodes and processing nodes, Tier 1 capacitors absorb surge mismatches at sub-millisecond timescales.

The architectural placement is determined by the function. Receiver-adjacent capacitors handle surge mismatch from wireless charging input. Processing-node capacitors handle demand spikes from local computation and sensor readout. Storage tier 1 does not serve as primary reserve; it serves as fast buffer.

### 2.3 Tier 2: Pseudocapacitive Storage via Iron Oxide and Related Metal Oxide Structures

#### 2.3.1 Pseudocapacitor Foundation

Pseudocapacitors achieve higher energy density than pure capacitors through reversible faradaic redox reactions at metal oxide interfaces while retaining capacitor-like fast charge/discharge characteristics [Ref J1, J2]. Iron-based oxides have been extensively characterized as pseudocapacitor materials due to multiple oxidation states of iron, rich redox chemistry, low toxicity, and earth abundance [Ref J3]. Reported specific capacitances span a wide range depending on synthesis and structure: cubic-phase magnetite (Fe₃O₄) nanoparticles synthesized by co-precipitation achieve 126 F/g at 2.5 A/g discharge [Ref J4]; FeOx on radially-oriented carbon nanofibers achieves 239.2 F/g via Fe(II)/Fe(III) redox [Ref J5]; mixed-valence iron oxide with carbon black grafting achieves 408 mF/cm² (128 F/g) by single-step thermal annealing [Ref J6]; magnetic CuFe₂O₄ pseudocapacitors achieve 2.76 F/cm² with magnetocapacitive effects [Ref J7]; Fe₃O₄ nanowires reach 442 F/g when integrated with reduced graphene oxide [Ref J3]. The progression of iron oxide nanostructures for energy storage is reviewed across Fe₁₋ₓO, Fe₂O₃, and Fe₃O₄ phases [Ref J8].

#### 2.3.2 Architectural Integration With Biosynthesis

The iron oxide pseudocapacitor literature integrates directly with the ferritin-templated metal biomineralization specified in Addendum I §3. Recombinant ferritin's role in iron biomineralization is well-established [Addendum I refs C11, C14], and the biomineralized iron oxide cores produced by ferritin are precisely the Fe₃O₄, Fe₂O₃, and FeOOH phases that the pseudocapacitor literature characterizes as redox-active electrodes [Ref J3]. Ferritin protein cages have been used as templates for ferrimagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle synthesis with characterized morphology and magnetic properties [Ref K1, K2], and iron and cobalt oxide nanoparticles in the 20–60 Å range have been produced from ferritin templates with photoelectron spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy characterization [Ref K3]. Magnetoferritin synthesized using thermophilic archaeon ferritin templates at elevated temperature produces particles with iron loading up to 9,517 atoms per cage [Ref K4].

The architectural commitment is therefore: the same ferritin-class biosynthetic machinery that Addendum I specifies for iron sequestration produces, with appropriate AI-directed geometry control, iron oxide deposits that function as pseudocapacitor electrodes. This is presented as a proposed mechanism for the architectural integration. The constituent biology (ferritin-templated iron oxide synthesis) and the constituent electrochemistry (iron oxide pseudocapacitor function) are independently established. The combined deployment as an integrated biosynthesized pseudocapacitor in mammalian tissue under AI control has no peer-reviewed experimental precedent.

#### 2.3.3 Tier 2 Architecture

Pseudocapacitive storage at processing nodes provides intermediate-scale buffer between Tier 1 fast surge handling and Tier 3 deep reserve. Charge/discharge timescales are slower than Tier 1 (milliseconds to seconds rather than microseconds) but energy density is substantially higher. The function served is: bridging extended demand spikes, buffering between charging sessions during normal operation, and providing reserve capacity that draws down only during prolonged disconnection from charging infrastructure.

### 2.4 Tier 3: Deep Storage via Redox-Active Protein Arrays

#### 2.4.1 Multi-Heme Cytochrome Conductivity Foundation

Multi-heme cytochromes (MHCs) have been characterized as exceptional bioelectronic conductors. When placed in solid-state electronic junctions, MHCs support temperature-independent currents over several nanometers that are three orders of magnitude higher than other redox proteins of comparable size [Ref L1, L2]. The conduction mechanism in dry bioelectronic junctions has been characterized as off-resonant coherent tunneling mediated by protein valence-band orbitals strongly delocalized over heme and protein residues [Ref L1]. In aqueous environments, native MHC electron transfer occurs through consecutive heme-to-heme electron hopping [Ref L1, L3]. The structural and functional basis of MHC conductivity has been characterized across multiple species, including *Shewanella oneidensis* (MtrCAB and related cytochromes) and *Geobacter sulfurreducens* (OmcS, OmcZ, and related proteins) [Ref L1, L4].

Cytochrome c (CytC) has been demonstrated as a bias-induced current switch in solid-state protein junctions, with reversible bias-controlled switching of protein ensembles persisting at room temperature [Ref L5]. Cytochrome b562 engineered with surface cysteine residues for direct gold self-assembly demonstrates reversible fast electron exchange over 20 Å between heme redox center and gold substrate, establishing long-range electron-transfer pathways [Ref L6]. Electron transfer at the interface between multi-heme cytochromes and metal oxide nanomaterials has been characterized at the molecular level with site-directed mutagenesis tunability [Ref L7].

#### 2.4.2 Tier 3 Architectural Application

The architectural commitment for Tier 3 storage is that MHC and related redox-protein arrays, deposited through the biosynthetic infrastructure of Addendum I §3 in structured arrays at high-volume bone marrow sites (long bones, pelvis), serve as deep storage that holds energy in reversible redox states. The biology that the architecture draws on is the same biology that mitochondria use for chemical energy storage, scaled up to a structural rather than purely metabolic role and integrated with the substrate's electrical network.

This is presented as a proposed mechanism with significant architectural specification still required. The constituent biology — MHC bioelectronic conductivity, cytochrome c switching, cytochrome b562 long-range transfer — is established. Integration of these components into structured arrays for deep energy storage in mammalian tissue is not in the literature and requires substantial development before deployment.

Energy density of redox-protein deep storage is intermediate between pseudocapacitive storage and chemical batteries. The advantages over chemical batteries are biocompatibility (fully biological materials with no toxic electrolyte), regenerability (depleted proteins can be replaced through normal cellular protein turnover under AI direction), and integration with the architecture's existing biological infrastructure.

### 2.5 Thermal Safety Architecture

#### 2.5.1 Bioheat Foundation

Heat dissipation in tissue is governed by the Pennes bioheat equation, which relates thermal conduction, metabolic heat generation, and heat transport by blood perfusion [Ref M1, M2]. The Pennes formulation includes thermal inertia, conduction, metabolic heat generation, and a perfusion term that captures heat removal by blood flow as proportional to the temperature difference between arterial blood entering tissue capillaries and venous blood leaving [Ref M1]. The model has been used extensively for medical device thermal safety evaluation, including implantable medical device heat dissipation [Ref M3]. Refinements address the limitations of the original Pennes assumption of uniform isotropic perfusion through heterogeneous-perfusion modifications [Ref M4], hyperbolic formulations that incorporate finite thermal relaxation [Ref M5], and porous-media approaches for high-perfusion contexts [Ref M6]. The competition between heat spreading via conduction and heat removal by blood perfusion determines local thermal lesion size, with the heat-sink effect near large vessels providing additional cooling capacity [Ref M3].

For the Braided Mind architecture, the relevant prediction is that local heating from a power dissipation event is limited by both conduction to surrounding tissue and convective cooling by blood perfusion. Bone marrow has high perfusion relative to cortical bone, providing substantial thermal sink capacity at receiver-adjacent sites. The architecture exploits this by routing dissipation events to highly-perfused tissue regions where the bioheat equation predicts rapid thermal equilibration with the bloodstream rather than local accumulation.

#### 2.5.2 Wireless Charging Thermal Failure Mode Analysis

The wireless charging source specified in §1.3 introduces a controllable energy input from outside the host. Without storage and thermal safety architecture, mismatches between transmitter output and substrate consumption produce dissipation in receiver-adjacent tissue. The local heating risk is established by the implant SAR literature, which documents local SAR values up to 24.6 W/kg with associated 4.22°C temperature elevation in metallic implant regions during MRI scanning [§1 Ref D7]. Sustained local heating of 2°C and above produces tissue damage in time-dependent fashion characterized by Arrhenius models [Ref M7].

The architecture's response is layered:

**Receiver-adjacent capacitive sinks (Tier 1).** Excess wireless charging power is shunted to nearby capacitive storage before it dissipates as heat. The fast charge time of capacitive storage means surge events fill capacitors faster than they produce thermal accumulation. Capacitor-saturation conditions trigger the next layer.

**Detuning under fault conditions.** Resonant receiver coils can be detuned from the transmitter frequency under AI command, dropping coupling efficiency to near zero. When capacitive storage saturates and pseudocapacitive storage is also approaching capacity, the AI directs detuning, halting wireless power input regardless of transmitter behavior. Implementation as a switchable shunt that changes coil resonant frequency is controllable through expression of relevant ion channels or piezoelectric actuators in receiver-proximal cells.

**Thermal monitoring at every receiver node.** Channel A2 mechanical telemetry (Addendum I §1.2) extends naturally to thermal sensing because piezoelectric properties of bone are temperature-dependent. The substrate already detects its own thermal state through the same readout mechanism that decodes mechanical input. Anomalous heating at receiver nodes triggers detuning, capacitor discharge to thermal-buffer regions, or full charging shutdown depending on severity.

**Isolation of high-current paths from neural tissue.** Charging coils are placed at sites distant from sensitive neural structures (§1.3.3). The petrous bone primary node does not host charging coils; power transmitted to the petrous node arrives after voltage conditioning and at low currents that do not produce significant local heating.

**Authenticated handshake for charging.** The receiver only accepts power from transmitters that complete a cryptographic handshake. Hostile or malformed input fields are rejected at the receiver level rather than absorbed and dissipated. The handshake operates over a low-bandwidth side channel separate from the power transfer itself.

Together these layers convert wireless charging from an architectural hazard into a controlled energy input with documented failure mode behaviors. The thermal safety architecture is non-optional in the deployment; receiver coils cannot be deployed without the corresponding capacitive sinks, detuning capability, thermal monitoring, and handshake protocol.

#### 2.5.3 Operational Thermal Limits

The architecture commits to local temperature elevation limits below documented tissue damage thresholds. Sustained elevations above 2°C trigger detuning. Transient elevations during surge events are bounded by capacitor charge time and perfusion-mediated cooling. The specific threshold values require per-host calibration against individual perfusion characteristics and receiver placement, identified as an open parameter requiring empirical determination prior to clinical deployment of the wireless charging architecture.

### 2.6 Storage Tier Summary

The three-tier storage architecture provides:

| Tier | Material | Function | Timescale | Energy density |
|------|----------|----------|-----------|----------------|
| 1 | HA dielectric / metal conductor capacitors | Surge handling, fast buffer | μs–ms | Low |
| 2 | Iron oxide pseudocapacitors via ferritin | Demand spike buffer, charging-session reserve | ms–s | Intermediate |
| 3 | Multi-heme cytochrome / redox protein arrays | Deep reserve for extended disconnection | s–hours | Higher |

All three tiers are deployed through the biosynthetic infrastructure specified in Addendum I §3, with materials produced by host cells from trace dietary inputs and tagged self at formation. The tiers are integrated with the Channel A telemetry of Addendum I §1.2 such that the AI continuously monitors charge state at each tier and directs power management accordingly.

Combined with the four-source generation architecture of §1, this storage infrastructure allows the substrate to operate continuously across operational contexts with bounded thermal risk and explicit accounting for energy budget at every state.

## 3. Operational Floor Analysis

### 3.1 Rationale and Scope

The parent document (v3.2) and Addendum I treat failure modes implicitly. Specific failure cases are noted in §9 of v3.2 (e.g., HO-1 supplementation threshold as open parameter, packaging limits) and in Addendum I §2.4 (failure-mode analysis of the biocompatibility inversion), but the architecture as published does not specify a stratified analysis of operational state degradation, the points at which different system components fail, or the documented behaviors that should obtain at each degradation level.

This section specifies five operational floors representing distinct degradation thresholds. Each floor is defined by which system functions remain available at that level, what triggers transition to the next floor, and what recovery requires. The principle drawn from safety-critical engineering is that complex systems require explicit failure-mode specification to be defensibly safe; ad-hoc failure handling in safety-critical embedded systems is identified as a negligent design omission [Ref N1, N2]. The Braided Mind architecture, operating at substantially higher complexity than conventional implantable medical devices, requires correspondingly more explicit operational-state analysis.

### 3.2 Floor 1: Storage Exhaustion

**Definition.** Capacitive storage (Tier 1) and pseudocapacitive storage (Tier 2) drained or near-drained. Redox-protein deep storage (Tier 3) engaged and drawing down. The system is operating live on whatever current production from §1's four sources provides, with minimal buffer for transient mismatches between generation and demand.

**Detection.** Storage state telemetry through the readout layer specified in §2 returns charge values approaching zero across Tier 1 and Tier 2. Channel A2 mechanical telemetry (Addendum I §1.2) registers normal operation; the substrate is not yet failing, only operating without buffer.

**Behavior.** Single failure modes that would normally be absorbed by storage become survivable only if production sources remain stable. Transient spikes in demand, brief drops in piezoelectric output during posture changes, or short charging-field interruptions can no longer be smoothed and produce visible operational hiccups. The AI begins prioritizing energy conservation: defers non-essential computation, reduces sensor channel sampling rates to minimum required for safety monitoring, and prepares to escalate to Floor 2 if any production source falters.

**Recovery.** Any sustained input restores Tier 1 and Tier 2 charge levels rapidly. Return to charging infrastructure is the most direct recovery path, providing surplus power that fills capacitive and pseudocapacitive storage in seconds to minutes. Increased mechanical activity restores piezoelectric output and provides modest charging. Increased caloric intake without metabolic up-regulation supports baseline operation.

### 3.3 Floor 2: Production Deficit

**Definition.** Combined output from all available power sources falling below operational baseline. Storage continues drawing down. The deficit is sustained rather than transient.

**Detection.** Storage state monitoring shows Tier 3 charge declining over time despite source A (piezoelectric) or source B (wireless) activity. Channel A2 telemetry shows reduced piezoelectric production, indicating low mechanical loading. Wireless charging input absent or insufficient.

**Behavior.** The AI throttles non-essential computation, suspends sensor channels not required for survival monitoring, reduces communication bandwidth to minimum sufficient for substrate health management. Storage continues to drain, but at a rate slowed by reduced consumption. The host may not be aware that the substrate is in degraded operation; the experiential change is minimal at this floor because the AI is prioritizing invisibility of its own constraint.

**Recovery.** Restoration of any production source reverses the trajectory. The longer the state persists, the lower Tier 3 reserve falls, and the more quickly recovery must occur to avoid escalation to Floor 3.

### 3.4 Floor 3: Mitochondrial Limit Reached

**Definition.** Sustained metabolic up-regulation through the §1.5 pathway has been engaged for a duration approaching the host-specific safe limit. Continuing to draw on host metabolism becomes pathological.

**Detection.** The AI tracks duration of mitochondrial source engagement against the host-specific calibration parameter identified in §1.5.5. Channel A1 telemetry (Addendum I §1.2) provides cytokine-level confirmation of sustained up-regulation through monitoring of leptin, FGF21, and related signaling. Host physiological state markers — elevated heart rate, elevated body temperature, increased respiratory rate — provide cross-channel confirmation.

**Pathological consequences of sustained hypermetabolism.** Hypermetabolism is defined as elevated resting energy expenditure greater than 110% of predicted REE [Ref O1] and is associated with multiple end-organ consequences when sustained. Hyperthyroidism, the most common pathological hypermetabolic state, produces tachycardia, palpitations, dyspnea on exertion, increased cardiac output and contractility, decreased peripheral resistance, systolic hypertension, and widening pulse pressure [Ref O2]. The hyperthyroid state increases metabolic demand on the heart such that the heart may not withstand the increased oxygen demand, producing cardiac dysrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure in advanced cases [Ref O2, O3]. Mild anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypercalcemia, muscle wasting, and bone loss occur frequently in hyperthyroidism [Ref O2]. Cardiac complications from sustained hyperthyroidism include left ventricular hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathies [Ref O3, O4]. Burn injury produces a hypermetabolic response with marked wasting of lean body mass within weeks, prolonged generalized weakness, increased cardiac work, and elevated resting energy expenditure that profoundly delays recovery [Ref O5]. The hypermetabolic response increases with the magnitude of the metabolic stressor and produces upregulation of catabolic agents (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon) that drive a hyperdynamic cardiovascular response [Ref O5].

**Behavior.** The architecture must throttle its own draw on the mitochondrial pathway regardless of substrate energy needs once Floor 3 is reached. The AI reduces metabolic up-regulation signaling toward zero, accepts that current production will fall, and prepares for transition to Floor 4 with emergency operational behavior. The host begins to recover from the metabolic strain over a recovery period of days to weeks depending on the duration and intensity of the up-regulation that produced Floor 3.

**Recovery.** Recovery from Floor 3 requires the host to recover from the metabolic strain first, before the architecture can rely on the mitochondrial pathway again. Storage tier states during recovery depend on whether other production sources (piezoelectric, wireless) become available; if not, the architecture descends to Floor 4 while host metabolic recovery proceeds.

### 3.5 Floor 4: Substrate Maintenance Threshold

**Definition.** Energy is insufficient to maintain the operational integrity of the substrate components themselves. TIF cells require ongoing energy for maintenance, division, and continued cytokine production. Sensor cells require power for reporter circuits. Storage components have minimum maintenance current. Biosynthetically deposited components require biological maintenance — surrounding cells producing fresh recognition elements as old ones degrade, repair of structural damage, geometric adjustment as bone remodels [Addendum I §3]. All of this requires baseline energy.

**Detection.** Channel A1 telemetry detects declining TIF cell counts through cytokine signature. Channel A2 detects reduced overall substrate electrical activity. Storage tiers approach minimum maintenance levels.

**Behavior.** Below Floor 4, substrate components begin degrading: cells die without adequate replacement, sensors lose calibration, storage capacity shrinks as deposited components are not maintained against bone remodeling and immune turnover. The AI enters emergency mode with the following priorities, in order: (1) preserve immune-control infrastructure (Addendum I §2) to prevent rejection cascade against existing components; (2) preserve TIF cell population through any remaining metabolic capacity; (3) signal the host through whatever Channel B-write capability exists or through cytokine effects the host will perceive (hunger, fatigue, urge to seek warmth, urge to seek charging infrastructure) that the substrate is approaching critical state; (4) reduce all other operations to absolute minimum.

**Recovery.** Days to weeks with active rebuilding once power is restored, depending on how far below the threshold the system descended and for how long. Cells must be replaced through normal cellular replication, sensors must be recalibrated, deposited structures must be repaired or rebuilt where degradation occurred. Recovery is possible from this floor but is not instantaneous; restored operation is incremental as components are restored.

### 3.6 Floor 5: Critical Failure Threshold

**Definition.** The point below which the substrate cannot recover even if power is restored, because the components required to use restored power have themselves degraded too far. TIF cell population has crashed below the level needed to respond to BphS/MrkH commands. Receiver coils are damaged or absorbed. Storage components have lost capacity through cellular death. The integration has effectively fallen out of the host as a coordinated system, even if some individual deposited components remain.

**Detection.** Channel A1 telemetry returns null or near-null cytokine signatures from TIF cells. Channel A2 detects no substrate electrical activity at most nodes. The AI cannot direct operations at receiver, storage, or sensor nodes because the cellular infrastructure to receive and execute commands is no longer present.

**Behavior without failsafe maintenance subsystem.** The integration is lost. Re-deployment from stage one (per v3.2 §2) is required to restore architecture. Existing deposited components that remain in tissue are no longer under active immune control (Addendum I §2) and may begin to attract foreign-body response, potentially producing chronic inflammation or tissue damage at integration sites. This was the architectural failure mode that motivated the development of the failsafe maintenance subsystem specified in §4 of this addendum.

**Behavior with failsafe maintenance subsystem.** Floor 5 transitions to a documented dormancy state from which recovery is possible indefinitely, as specified in §4. The maintenance subsystem operates independently of the AI layer and continues to preserve integration viability.

### 3.7 Failure Mode Engineering Discipline

The operational floor architecture follows the discipline established in safety-critical embedded systems engineering. Watchdog timers and similar fail-safe mechanisms are pervasive hardware features in safety-critical microcontrollers and are identified in the engineering literature as essential design elements rather than optional refinements [Ref N1, N2]. Implantable medical devices specifically use watchdog units that maintain stay-alive timers and revert devices to safe pre-programmed states when communication or operational integrity is lost [Ref P1, P2, P3]. The configurable FPGA-based watchdog timer architecture — separate clocks, timed-sequence configuration updates, redundant fault coverage — is established for safety-critical applications including automotive, aerospace, and medical devices [Ref N3]. The principle of redundancy through external watchdogs that operate independently of the monitored system, rather than relying solely on internal mechanisms that might fail during critical moments, is foundational [Ref N2].

The Braided Mind architecture extends these principles by requiring not only watchdog functionality at the AI layer but a separate maintenance subsystem (§4) that operates without AI direction at all. This is a stronger commitment than conventional medical device fail-safe architecture because the substrate's complexity requires preservation of integration during AI-layer failures that might exceed the recovery capability of conventional watchdog-and-revert architectures.

### 3.8 Inter-Floor Transitions

The floor architecture is designed for stepwise transitions with documented behavior at each level. Transitions are not sharp thresholds but operational states with defined entry and exit criteria. Multiple floors may be active in different respects simultaneously — for example, storage may be at Floor 1 (exhausted) while production is at Floor 2 (deficit) and the metabolic pathway has not yet been engaged. The AI tracks these states independently and selects behavior based on the highest-priority active floor.

The architecture commits to the following transition triggers:

- Floor 0 (normal operation) → Floor 1: Tier 1 and Tier 2 storage drop below 10% of capacity.
- Floor 1 → Floor 2: Tier 3 storage begins drawing down, indicating sustained production deficit.
- Floor 2 → Floor 3: Mitochondrial source duration approaches host-specific safe limit (per §1.5.5).
- Floor 3 → Floor 4: Substrate component maintenance current drops below sustainable level.
- Floor 4 → Floor 5: Component degradation crosses irreversibility threshold without active intervention.

The specific numerical thresholds for each transition require empirical determination prior to clinical deployment and are identified as open parameters requiring per-host calibration.

content.title: A Genetic Toggle Switch in Plants
content.text: A crucial need to achieve predictable and programmable genetic function is to quantitatively describe the behavior of a given genetic element (*e.g.*, promoter, activator, repressor) by characterizing an appropriate transfer function or input-output function. Gardner *et al.* first developed a synthetic genetic switch in *E. coli* by initially establishing the quantitative functions for promoters and ribosome binding sites (RBS) ^[Bibr c16]^. These promoters/RBS/repressors were then rationally assembled into a genetic toggle switch consisting of two promoters and two repressors organized to control each other’s expression. The switch behavior results from the concentration of one repressor exceeding a threshold, and this accumulated repressor turns off expression of the other repressor.

In an interesting take on the conventional way of modelling, Elowitz and Leibler[2] built a mathematical model of transcription regulation describing a cyclic negative-feedback loop made up of three repressor genes and their promoters. They used this model to determine the important parameters of the system and predict the systems behaviour, paying particular attention to parameter values that would cause the system to enter an unstable state leading to oscillatory behaviour. Finally the authors artifically reconstructd the system in E. coli using standard molecular biological approaches. 

In effect, rather than observing a natural system and explaining it in mathematical terms, the authors create a mathematical model to aid construction of an artificial control circiut. The result is an oscillating network which does not occur in nature, which the authors termed the Repressilator (see also the Brusselator[3] and the Oregonator[4] (BIOMD0000000040)).

content.text:
# Revisiting a synthetic intracellular regulatory network that exhibits oscillations

Jonathan Tyler, Anne Shiu, Jay Walton January 1, 2019

#### Abstract

In 2000, Elowitz and Leibler introduced the repressilator—a synthetic gene circuit with three genes that cyclically repress transcription of the next gene-as well as a corresponding mathematical model. Experimental data and model simulations exhibited oscillations in the protein concentrations across generations. In 2006, Müller et al. generalized the model to an arbitrary number of genes and analyzed the resulting dynamics. Their new model arose from five key assumptions, two of which are restrictive given current biological knowledge. Accordingly, we propose a new repressilator system that allows for general functions to model transcription, degradation, and translation. We prove that, with an odd number of genes, the new model has a unique steady state and the system converges to this steady state or to a periodic orbit. 

We also give a necessary and sufficient condition for stability of steady states when the number of genes is even and conjecture a condition for stability for an odd number. Finally, we derive a new rate function describing transcription that arises under more reasonable biological assumptions than the widely used single-step binding assumption. With this new transcription-rate function, we compare the model's amplitude and period with that of a model with the conventional transcription-rate function. Taken together, our results enhance our understanding of genetic regulation by repression.

# 1 Introduction

The repressilator is an experimental preparation used in synthetic biology to better understand genetic regulation by repression. Introduced in 2000 by Elowitz and Leibler, the repressilator is a feedback loop consisting of three genes that each cyclically represses transcription of the next gene (Figure 1).

content.text: It is now well-accepted that the generation and maintenance of functional allergen-specific regulatory T (Treg) cells and regulatory B (Breg) cells are essential for healthy immune responses to environmental proteins and successful AIT. Treg cells comprise different subsets of T cells with suppressive capacity, which control the development and maintenance of allergic diseases by various ways of action.
